Quantum Geometric Tensor Preconditioning for Stable Training of Recurrent Neural Quantum States

Adil Attar Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON N2L 3G1, Canada    Amine M. Aboussalah Affiliation: NYU Tandon School of Engineering, 6 MetroTech Center, Brooklyn, New York 11201, United States    Mohamed Hibat-Allah Email: mohamed.hibatallah@uwaterloo.ca Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON N2L 3G1, Canada Affiliation: Vector Institute, Toronto, Ontario, M5G 0C6, Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Neural Quantum States (NQS) provide a powerful neural network–based variational framework for representing many-body wave functions and solving for ground states. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are particularly promising owing to their relatively low computational cost and their autoregressive property, which enables perfect sampling. Recently, RNNs have been reported to be unstable under curvature-based optimizers such as the minimum-step stochastic reconfiguration (minSR) method. In this paper, we address this perceived limitation and show that minSR can be stabilized through simple regularization techniques, enabling robust training of RNN-based NQS with only a few samples. Our approach outperforms the Adam optimizer on the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model and the one-dimensional cluster state, and provides competitive results on the two-dimensional Heisenberg and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} models. This work offers a promising pathway for using modern optimization techniques with autoregressive NQS to address open questions in quantum simulation.

I Introduction

Simulating quantum matter with neural-network quantum states (NQS) is an emerging field that has delivered promising results in the quantum matter community [1, 2, 3]. This achievement has been enabled by different neural network architectures ranging from restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) [1, 4, 5, 6, 7], feedforward neural networks [8, 9], convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [10, 11, 12], to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21] and Transformer-based wave functions [22, 23, 24, 25, 26] for benchmarks beyond ground state physics, ranging from real-time quantum dynamics of pure states [1, 27, 28, 29, 30], dynamics of open quantum systems [31, 32, 33], to thermal quantum many-body physics [34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. A cornerstone principle enabling these advances is the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) framework [39], where one minimizes the variational energy, i.e., the expectation value of a Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} in a variational wave function |Ψ𝜽⟩|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle with parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}, in the particular task of ground state approximation. This minimization has largely been performed in the NQS community using gradient descent through either first-order or second-order optimization techniques. One of the most effective methods is stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [40, 39], a second-order optimization method known in the machine-learning literature as natural gradient [41]. This technique is well-principled thanks to its correspondence to imaginary time evolution [40, 39, 42, 43]. This method has been extended to its minimal counterpart: minimum-step stochastic reconfiguration (minSR) [12, 24], which provides a significant speedup when the number of samples is small compared to the total number of variational parameters.

Second-order optimization has remained largely unexplored for RNNs due to its reported ill-conditioning [44, 45, 38, 46]. This challenge is mainly related to the rapid decay of the spectrum of the Fisher matrix, which makes its inversion an ill-defined problem. For this architecture, the first-order Adam optimizer [47] is currently the most widely used choice, with promising results in ground state benchmarks [14, 20]. Recently, the natural gradient optimization approach with autoregressive models has seen some success in the context of classical statistical physics [48] and ab-initio quantum chemistry [49]. Thus, a natural question is whether it is possible to stabilize the optimization of RNN wave functions using minSR despite previous reports of instability in the NQS literature. A second important question is whether a subsampled Fisher matrix in minSR with few samples still provides a useful preconditioner during optimization. In this work, we address both questions and develop a reproducible stability framework for minSR applied to RNN wave functions on prototypical one- and two-dimensional quantum benchmarks, supported by conditioning analysis, Fisher spectrum diagnostics, and controlled ablations. In particular, we demonstrate a significant advantage over the Adam optimizer in one spatial dimension on the ferromagnetic transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and cluster state benchmarks. In two spatial dimensions, we show that minSR can be made stable and comparable to the Adam optimizer on the square lattice Heisenberg and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} models. Our results also show a speed-up in convergence for minSR optimization. Additionally, all of our investigations were conducted using only a few hundred Monte Carlo samples on a single GPU, highlighting the computational efficiency of RNN wave functions.

II Methods

II.1 Recurrent Neural Network wave function

We use RNNs as a variational quantum many-body wave function [13] over a lattice of spins 𝝈\bm{\sigma}, written as

|Ψ𝜽⟩=∑𝝈Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)​|𝝈⟩.\displaystyle\ket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}=\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\ket{\bm{\sigma}}. (1)

In the computational basis, an RNN wave function can be expressed as

Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=P𝜽​(𝝈)​exp⁡[i​ϕ𝜽​(𝝈)],\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sqrt{P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})}\exp{\bigl[i\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\bigr]}, (2)

where 𝝈=(σ1,…,σN)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{N}) denotes the lattice-spin configuration and each σi\sigma_{i} can take one of dσd_{\sigma} possible values, with dσ=2d_{\sigma}=2 for spin-12\frac{1}{2} systems. 𝜽\bm{\theta} is the set of variational parameters, which includes the weights and biases of our RNN. P𝜽​(𝝈)P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) is the probability distribution over the spins, and ϕ𝜽​(𝝈)\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) is the phase of the wave function.

RNN wave functions stand out for their ability to autoregressively sample P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}}. This procedure is performed by decomposing P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}} using the chain rule of probabilities as

P𝜽​(𝝈)=P𝜽​(σ1)​P𝜽​(σ2|σ1)​…​P𝜽​(σN|σ1,…,σN−1),P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{1})P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{2}|\sigma_{1})\dots P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{N}|\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{N-1}), (3)

and directly modeling these conditional probabilities, which are univariate multinomial distributions that can be directly sampled. Through the process of sampling each conditional probability P𝜽​(σi|σ<i)P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i}), an RNN wave function can efficiently produce uncorrelated samples for estimating observables and avoid Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) schemes [13, 50]. The phases of the wave function can be decomposed similarly

ϕ⁡(𝝈)=∑iϕi​(σi|σ<i),\phi(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{i}\phi_{i}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i}), (4)

where the conditional phases ϕi\phi_{i} and the conditional probabilities are calculated using the RNN output (shown in Fig. 1(a)), and their exact form depends on the specific RNN architecture. RNNs make the core assumption that a hidden state 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} can effectively summarize all previously seen spins, such that

P𝜽​(σi|σ<i)=P𝜽​(σi|𝒉i),\displaystyle P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i})=P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\bm{h}_{i}), (5)
ϕ⁡(𝝈)=∑iϕi​(σi|𝒉i).\displaystyle\phi(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{i}\phi_{i}(\sigma_{i}|\bm{h}_{i}). (6)

We depict the RNN wave function generally in Fig. 1(a). Here we can define two types of RNN wave functions [13], positive RNN (pRNN) wave functions, which do not include a phase term and are applicable in the case of stoquastic Hamiltonians [13, 20]. A second class is the complex RNN (cRNN) wave function, which includes both a probability and a phase term and can model ground states of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians [13, 19]. Note that the conditional probabilities are given by

P𝜽​(σi|σ<i)=softmax​(U​𝒉i+𝒄)⋅𝝈i,P_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i})=\textrm{softmax}(U\bm{h}_{i}+\bm{c})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i}, (7)

where 𝝈i\bm{\sigma}_{i} is the one-hot encoding of σi\sigma_{i}, and 𝒉i∈ℝdh\bm{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} is the hidden state, with dimension dhd_{h}. U∈ℝdσ×dhU\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}\times d_{h}} and 𝒄∈ℝdσ\bm{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} are learnable parameters, and softmax is given by

softmax⁡(𝒙)i=exi∑kexk.\displaystyle\operatorname{softmax}(\bm{x})_{i}=\frac{e^{x_{i}}}{\sum_{k}e^{x_{k}}}. (8)

By applying a softmax activation, our conditional probabilities become normalized, and by extension our wave function becomes normalized [13]. Furthermore, the conditional phases are given by

ϕi=π​Softsign​(Uϕ​𝒉i+𝒄ϕ)⋅𝝈i,\displaystyle\phi_{i}=\pi\textrm{Softsign}(U_{\phi}\bm{h}_{i}+\bm{c}_{\phi})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i}, (9)

where the Softsign function is given by

Softsign⁡(𝒙)i=xi1+|xi|∈(−1,1).\displaystyle\operatorname{Softsign}(\bm{x})_{i}=\frac{x_{i}}{1+|x_{i}|}\in(-1,1). (10)

For the simplest RNN cell, known as a vanilla RNN cell [51], the hidden state is updated as

𝒉i=f⁡(W⁡[𝒉i−1;𝝈i−1]+𝒃),\bm{h}_{i}=f(W[\bm{h}_{i-1};\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}]+\bm{b}){\color[rgb]{0,0,1},} (11)

where W∈ℝdh×(dh+dσ)W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times(d_{h}+d_{\sigma})} and 𝒃∈ℝdh\bm{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} are all learnable parameters, ff is a non-linear activation function, and [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] represents vector concatenation. We initialize the hidden state 𝒉0\bm{h}_{0} and the first input 𝝈0\bm{\sigma}_{0} as zero vectors. The same parameters are shared across every spin in the lattice, making RNNs ideal for transfer learning across different sizes [16, 14, 18, 19].

For simplicity, we present the vanilla RNN cell implementation, and we refer to App. A for a detailed implementation of the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) cell used in this work, which can better capture long-range dependencies in our lattice compared to vanilla RNNs [14]. Dilated recurrent connections have also been proposed to inject a long-range inductive bias into RNN wave functions and to help reproduce power-law correlations [52].

II.2 Two-dimensional RNNs

RNN wave functions can be extended to two-dimensional systems [13] as depicted in Fig. 1(b). In this setup, each RNN cell receives inputs from the horizontal and vertical neighbors. To maintain the autoregressive property, we define a one-dimensional path π⁡(k)\pi(k), with k∈[0,Nx​Ny−1]k\in[0,N_{x}N_{y}-1], that goes through all the spins in our lattice. We choose a zigzag path

π⁡(k)=(ik,jk),\pi(k)=(i_{k},j_{k}),\\ (12)

where jk=⌊k/Nx⌋j_{k}=\lfloor k/N_{x}\rfloor and

ik={kmodNxif jk is even(Nx−1)−(kmodNx)if jk is odd.i_{k}=\begin{cases}k\mod{N_{x}}&\textrm{if $j_{k}$ is even}\\ (N_{x}-1)-(k\mod{N_{x}})&\textrm{if $j_{k}$ is odd}\end{cases}. (13)

The conditional probabilities are given by

P𝜽​(𝝈π⁡(k)|𝝈π(<k))=softmax​(U​𝒉i,j+𝒄)⋅𝝈i,j,P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}_{\pi(k)}|\bm{\sigma}_{\pi(<k)})=\textrm{softmax}(U\bm{h}_{i,j}+\bm{c})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i,j}, (14)

with π⁡(k)=(i,j)\pi(k)=(i,j). π(<k)\pi(<k) corresponds to all spins generated before 𝝈i,j\bm{\sigma}_{i,j} with respect to the zigzag path as depicted in Fig. 1(b). Note that the bias introduced by the zigzag sampling path can be mitigated by applying symmetries, which results in an improved accuracy in a variational calculation [13, 14]. The conditional phases for the two-dimensional RNN can be defined similarly to the one-dimensional case;

ϕi,j=π​Softsign​(Uϕ​𝒉i,j+𝒄ϕ)⋅𝝈i,j.\displaystyle\phi_{i,j}=\pi\textrm{Softsign}(U_{\phi}\bm{h}_{i,j}+\bm{c}_{\phi})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i,j}. (15)

In its simplest version, the 2D RNN wave function’s hidden states are given by

𝒉i​j=f⁡(W⁡[𝝈i−(−1)j,j;𝝈i,j−1;𝒉i−(−1)j,j;𝒉i,j−1]+𝐛).\displaystyle\bm{h}_{ij}=f(W[\bm{\sigma}_{i-(-1)^{j},j};\bm{\sigma}_{i,j-1};\bm{h}_{i-(-1)^{j},j};\bm{h}_{i,j-1}]+\mathbf{b}). (16)

Here ff is a non-linear activation function, and W∈ℝdh×2​(dσ+dh)W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times 2(d_{\sigma}+d_{h})} and 𝒃∈ℝdh\bm{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} are learnable parameters. Boundary spins and hidden states are initialized with the zero vector. In this work, we use a GRU variant of this two-dimensional architecture, which we describe in detail in App. A.

II.3 Optimization

To optimize the parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} of our normalized RNN wave function, we apply the variational principle and minimize the energy expectation value ⟨H^⟩\braket{\hat{H}}:

minθ⁡⟨Ψ𝜽|H^|Ψ𝜽⟩≳EG​S,\min_{\theta}\braket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}\gtrsim E_{GS}, (17)

where EG​SE_{GS} is the true ground state energy for the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}. We define the local energy ϵ⁡(𝝈)\epsilon(\bm{\sigma}) of our wave function as

ϵ⁡(𝝈)=∑𝝈′H𝝈​𝝈′​Ψ𝜽​(𝝈′)Ψ𝜽​(𝝈),\displaystyle\epsilon(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\frac{H_{\bm{\sigma}\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})}{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})}, (18)

where H𝝈​𝝈′=⟨𝝈|H^|𝝈′⟩H_{\bm{\sigma}\bm{\sigma^{\prime}}}=\braket{\bm{\sigma}|\hat{H}|\bm{\sigma^{\prime}}}. We can rewrite the energy expectation value as an average over the probability distribution P𝜽​(𝝈)=|Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)|2P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2} [39]

⟨H^⟩=\displaystyle\braket{\hat{H}}= ∑𝝈|Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)|2​∑𝝈′H𝝈​𝝈′​Ψ𝜽​(𝝈′)Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}\sum_{\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\frac{H_{\bm{\sigma}\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}^{\prime})}{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})} (19)
=\displaystyle= ∑𝝈P𝜽​(𝝈)​ϵ​(𝝈).\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\epsilon(\bm{\bm{\sigma}}). (20)

The summation is over all possible spin configurations, whose number grows exponentially with the number of spins. Notably, our RNN wave function has the autoregressive property, which allows us to perfectly sample a list of configurations 𝝈(1)​…​𝝈(Ns)\bm{\sigma}^{(1)}\ldots\bm{\sigma}^{(N_{s})} efficiently [13]. As a result, our energy expectation value can be estimated as

E𝜽=1Ns​∑i=1Nsϵ⁡(𝝈(i)).\displaystyle E_{\bm{\theta}}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}\epsilon(\bm{\sigma}^{(i)}). (21)

The parameters of Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}} can be updated as 𝜽→𝜽−δ​𝜽\bm{\theta}\rightarrow\bm{\theta}-\delta\bm{\theta} using stochastic gradient descent (SGD), with δ​𝜽\delta\bm{\theta} being the direction of steepest descent

δ​𝜽\displaystyle\delta\bm{\theta} =η​∂𝜽E𝜽,\displaystyle=\eta\partial_{\bm{\theta}}E_{\bm{\theta}}, (22)
≈2η1Ns∑i=1NsRe[∂𝜽logΨ(𝝈(i))ϵ(𝝈(i))∗].\displaystyle\approx 2\eta\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}\operatorname{Re}\Bigr[\partial_{\bm{\theta}}\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(i)})\epsilon(\bm{\sigma}^{(i)})^{*}\Bigl]. (23)

Here η\eta is the step-size for our optimization. We define 𝒪k​s≡1Ns​∂𝜽klog⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈(s))\mathcal{O}_{ks}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\partial_{\bm{\theta}_{k}}\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}). We can further reduce the noise in the gradients by centering ϵ\epsilon, with ϵ¯i=1Ns​(ϵ⁡(𝝈(i))−E)∗\bar{\epsilon}_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}_{s}}(\epsilon(\bm{\sigma}^{(i)})-E)^{*} [13].

δ𝜽=2ηRe[𝒪ϵ¯].\displaystyle\delta\bm{\theta}=2\eta\operatorname{Re}\Bigr[\mathcal{O}\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}\Bigl]. (24)

Both the local energy ϵ∈ℂNs\bm{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{s}} and the log-derivative matrix 𝒪∈ℂNp×Ns\mathcal{O}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{p}\times N_{s}} are estimated by sampling the variational wave function NsN_{s} times in parallel at every training iteration.

Several variants of SGD have been developed to help accelerate convergence. Momentum can add information from previous gradient steps, making optimization more robust against noise [53]. Several sophisticated momentum-inspired versions of SGD have been developed, such as Adam [47], which is among the state of the art in first-order optimization. Although first-order methods can perform well, they may make slow progress through flat regions of the loss landscape [54]. These flat plateaus are ubiquitous in neural networks, as they arise from their highly degenerate parameterization [55]. To overcome these issues, we explore Natural Gradient Descent as a viable optimization alternative.

II.4 Natural Gradients

Natural Gradient, otherwise known as SR in the VMC community [39], is a curvature-based method to optimize a variational ansatz. Its main advantage is the ability to escape flat plateaus in the loss landscape in finite time [54]. For statistical models, the Fisher information matrix is the Hessian of the Kullback–Leibler divergence, i.e. the Bregman divergence generated by the negative entropy, and the natural gradient is the ordinary gradient preconditioned by its inverse. In the context of VMC, the natural gradient can be viewed in two equivalent ways: as approximating imaginary-time evolution [2], or using a geometric point of view by minimizing the Fubini-Study metric during updates [39]. We proceed by deriving Natural Gradients from the imaginary-time evolution view. Given a trial wave function Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}, the natural gradient update approximates the imaginary-time evolution

|Ψ𝜽−δ​𝜽⟩=exp⁡(−H^​δ​τ)​|Ψ𝜽⟩,\ket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}-\delta\bm{\theta}}}=\exp{(-\hat{H}\delta\tau)}\ket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}, (25)

which exponentially suppresses all excited states relative to the ground state. We Taylor expand both the wave function and the imaginary-time evolution to first order

|Ψ𝜽⟩−δ​𝜽⋅∇𝜽|Ψ𝜽⟩=|Ψ𝜽⟩−δ​τ​H^​|Ψ𝜽⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle-\delta\bm{\theta}\cdot\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle=|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle-\delta\tau\hat{H}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle. (26)

Normalized imaginary-time evolution gives

|Ψ𝜽⟩⟶|Ψ𝜽⟩−δ​τ​(H^−E𝜽)​|Ψ𝜽⟩.|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle\longrightarrow|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle-\delta\tau(\hat{H}-E_{\bm{\theta}})|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle.

Matching this tangent vector to the normalized version of the variational displacement −δ𝜽⋅∇𝜽|Ψ𝜽⟩-\delta\bm{\theta}\cdot\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle in a Fubini–Study metric minimization task leads to

δ​𝜽=argminδ​𝜽∈ℝNp‖𝒪¯𝖳​δ​𝜽−2​η​ϵ¯∗‖22,\displaystyle\delta\bm{\theta}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\|\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\bm{\theta}-2\eta\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}, (27)

where 𝒪¯k​s=𝒪k​s−1Ns​∑s′𝒪k​s′\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ks}=\mathcal{O}_{ks}-\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s^{\prime}}\mathcal{O}_{ks^{\prime}} and η=δ​τ/2\eta=\delta\tau/2 serves the role of the learning rate [56]. Since this system is under-determined, we add Tikhonov regularization,

argminδ​𝜽∈ℝNp‖𝒪¯𝖳​δ​𝜽−2​η​ϵ¯∗‖22+λ​‖δ​𝜽‖22.\operatorname*{argmin}_{\delta\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{p}}}\|\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\bm{\theta}-2\eta\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\delta\bm{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}. (28)

For a complex-valued ansatz, this least-squares problem can be written exactly as a real one by defining

𝒪¯′\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime} =(Re⁡𝒪¯​Im⁡𝒪¯),\displaystyle=\Bigl(\,\operatorname{Re}\bar{\mathcal{O}}\;\;\operatorname{Im}\bar{\mathcal{O}}\,\Bigr), (29)
ϵ¯′\displaystyle\bm{\bar{\epsilon}}^{\prime} =2​(Re⁡ϵ¯−Im⁡ϵ¯).\displaystyle=2\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}\bm{\bar{\epsilon}}\\ -\operatorname{Im}\bm{\bar{\epsilon}}\end{pmatrix}. (30)

The normal equations are therefore

δ​𝜽=η​(S+λ​𝕀)−1​𝒪¯′​ϵ¯′,S≡𝒪¯′​𝒪𝖳′¯=Re⁡(𝒪¯​𝒪¯†),\delta\bm{\theta}=\eta\big(S+\lambda\mathbb{I}\big)^{-1}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime}\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{\prime},\qquad S\equiv\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime}\bar{\mathcal{O}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}}=\operatorname{Re}\big(\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\big), (31)

where λ\lambda is a Tikhonov parameter to mitigate ill-conditioning, and can be interpreted as an inverse trust region radius. When λ≫‖S‖\lambda\gg\|S\| the updates approach the SGD updates in Eq. (24) with centered log-derivatives. The complex matrix Q≡𝒪¯​𝒪¯†Q\equiv\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} is the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), while for real parameters the Fubini–Study metric entering SR is its real part SS. For a positive real ansatz, the imaginary blocks vanish, and the two definitions coincide. SR is therefore a natural-gradient method: parameter updates are measured by the distance between quantum states rather than by the Euclidean distance between parameters.

Using the identity (A​A𝖳+λ​I)−1​A=A​(A𝖳​A+λ​I)−1(AA^{\mathsf{T}}+\lambda I)^{-1}A=A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A+\lambda I)^{-1} gives the minSR update

δ​𝜽=η​𝒪¯′​(𝒯+λ​𝕀)−1​ϵ¯′,𝒯≡𝒪¯𝖳′​𝒪¯′,\delta\bm{\theta}=\eta\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime}\big(\mathcal{T}+\lambda\mathbb{I}\big)^{-1}\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{\prime},\qquad\mathcal{T}\equiv\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime}, (32)

which is the real-parameter form of the minSR identity used in our implementation. For a complex-valued ansatz, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is 2​Ns×2​Ns2N_{s}\times 2N_{s}; for a positive real ansatz, the zero imaginary block can be omitted, and the reduced matrix is Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s}. In either case, minSR replaces the parameter-space inversion by a sample-space inversion, reducing the leading inversion cost from cubic in NpN_{p} to 𝒪⁡(Ns2​Np+Ns3)\mathcal{O}(N_{s}^{2}N_{p}+N_{s}^{3}) up to constant factors. Geometrically, minSR is the natural-gradient update restricted to the sample-spanned tangent subspace. In this study, we work in the Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p} regime, and we find the Jacobian calculation to be the most memory-consuming step, with leading time complexity O⁡(dh2​N​Ns)O(d_{h}^{2}NN_{s}). We present the minSR algorithm in Algorithm II.4 and apply momentum as described in App. B.

II.5 RNN Fisher Spectrum

Natural-gradient optimization of RNN wave functions can be challenging due to two main considerations. First, different RNN parameter values can describe the same wave function. Directions that leave the wave function itself unchanged have zero Fisher norm and therefore appear as exact zero modes of the Fisher matrix. Second, the RNN recurrence can amplify small parameter changes, which can produce very large Fisher eigenvalues. Together, these two effects can spread the Fisher spectrum over a wide range and make the SR matrix severely ill-conditioned.

Fisher singularities from redundant parameters are not unique to RNN wave functions: in transformer manifolds, low Fisher rank similarly identifies locally inactive parameter directions and motivates intrinsic-dimension-aware adaptation [57]. A related interaction between architecture and representation geometry appears in message-passing networks, where local graph topology can determine whether repeated propagation yields expressive representations or oversmoothing [58].

We now state both mechanisms as propositions. The proofs can be found in App. C for a simplified model: a real, positive, autoregressive RNN wave function over NN sites, whose conditional distributions are produced by a linear RNN cell with a softmax head. At site ii, the hidden state 𝐡i∈ℝdh\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} and the logits 𝐳i∈ℝdσ\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} obey 𝐡i=W​𝐡i−1+V​𝝈i+𝐛\mathbf{h}_{i}=W\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+V\bm{\sigma}_{i}+\mathbf{b} and 𝐳i=U​𝐡i−1+𝐜\mathbf{z}_{i}=U\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+\mathbf{c}. Here 𝝈i∈ℝdσ\bm{\sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} is the one-hot encoding of the local spin, W∈ℝdh×dhW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{h}} is the recurrent matrix, V∈ℝdh×dσV\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{\sigma}} is the input matrix, U∈ℝdσ×dhU\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}\times d_{h}} is the readout matrix, and 𝐛∈ℝdh\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, 𝐜∈ℝdσ\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} are biases. The initial hidden state is fixed at 𝐡0=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}. The conditional probability vector at site ii is 𝐩i=softmax⁡(𝐳i)\mathbf{p}_{i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{i}). These exact G​L​(dh)GL(d_{h}) gauge statements are proved for this linear model; a gated nonlinear GRU does not, in general, possess the same full hidden-basis symmetry exactly.

Proposition 1 (Exact gauge degeneracy)

Consider the previous linear RNN wave function, with parameters 𝛉=(W,V,𝐛,U,𝐜)\bm{\theta}=(W,V,\mathbf{b},U,\mathbf{c}) and fixed initial hidden state 𝐡0=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}. Fix any matrix X∈ℝdh×dhX\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{h}} and define the parameter velocities

𝜽˙X=([X,W],X​V,X​𝐛,−U​X, 0),\dot{\bm{\theta}}_{X}=\big([X,W],\,XV,\,X\mathbf{b},\,-UX,\,\mathbf{0}\big), (33)

whose five entries are the increments of W,V,𝐛,U,𝐜W,V,\mathbf{b},U,\mathbf{c}, and where [X,W]=X​W−W​X[X,W]=XW-WX is the commutator, or Lie bracket, of XX and WW. Then d​𝛉X=𝛉˙X​d​td\bm{\theta}_{X}=\dot{\bm{\theta}}_{X}\text{d}t, given a real-valued parameter tt, is a symmetry direction of the model, with two consequences:

  1. (i)

    It leaves the wave function unchanged. The directional derivative of log⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) along d​𝜽Xd\bm{\theta}_{X} is zero for every configuration 𝝈\bm{\sigma}, not just on average.

  2. (ii)

    It is therefore a null direction of the SR matrix S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}. It lies in ker⁡S\ker S both for the finite-sample matrix built from any set of configurations and for its population limit (Ns→∞N_{s}\to\infty) under sampling from |Ψ𝜽|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}.

The directions d​𝛉Xd\bm{\theta}_{X} are the infinitesimal generators of the gauge group G​L​(dh)GL(d_{h}) of invertible real dh×dhd_{h}\times d_{h} matrices, which act on the parameters through Eq. (62). Equivalently, the tangent space to the gauge orbit at 𝛉\bm{\theta} is contained in ker⁡S\ker S.

The proof is given in App. C.

Proposition 2 (Recurrent amplification)

Consider the model of Proposition 1, now with a diagonal recurrent matrix W=diag⁡(r1,…,rdh)W=\operatorname{diag}(r_{1},\dots,r_{d_{h}}), so that the hidden modes evolve independently with multipliers r1,…,rdhr_{1},\dots,r_{d_{h}}. Let SS be the population SR matrix, i.e. the Ns→∞N_{s}\to\infty limit of 𝒪¯​𝒪¯†\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} under configurations drawn i.i.d. from |Ψ𝛉|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}. Since SS is Hermitian and positive semidefinite, its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative; we write λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S) for the largest one.

Fix a hidden mode a∈{1,…,dh}a\in\{1,\dots,d_{h}\}, and let 𝐮a=U​𝐞a\mathbf{u}_{a}=U\mathbf{e}_{a} be its readout vector, with 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a} the aa-th standard basis vector of ℝdh\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}. Define the nonnegative quantity

χa,i=⟨𝐮a𝖳​Ci​𝐮a⟩≥ 0,\chi_{a,i}=\big\langle\mathbf{u}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{i}\,\mathbf{u}_{a}\big\rangle\;\geq\;0, (34)

which measures the conditional softmax covariance Ci=diag⁡(𝐩i)−𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳C_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{p}_{i})-\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}} at site ii along the readout direction 𝐮a\mathbf{u}_{a}, averaged over histories drawn from |Ψ𝛉|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}. Assume uniform non-saturation: there is a constant χ0>0\chi_{0}>0 with χa,i≥χ0\chi_{a,i}\geq\chi_{0} for all sites i≤Ni\leq N and all system sizes NN.

Then λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S) diverges with NN, at a rate set by the multiplier rar_{a}:

  1. (i)

    Marginal mode (ra=1r_{a}=1).

    λmax​(S)≥χ04​(N−1)​N​(2​N−1)6,\lambda_{\max}(S)\;\geq\;\frac{\chi_{0}}{4}\,\frac{(N-1)N(2N-1)}{6}, (35)

    which grows as χ0​N3/12\chi_{0}N^{3}/12: polynomial in the system size NN.

  2. (ii)

    Expanding mode (|ra|>1|r_{a}|>1).

    λmax​(S)≥14​|mN−1​(ra)|2​χa,N,\lambda_{\max}(S)\;\geq\;\frac{1}{4}\,\big|m_{N-1}(r_{a})\big|^{2}\,\chi_{a,N}, (36)

    with mN−1​(ra)=(1−raN−1)/(1−ra)m_{N-1}(r_{a})=(1-r_{a}^{\,N-1})/(1-r_{a}). The right-hand side grows as |ra|2​(N−1)​χa,N/(4​|ra−1|2)|r_{a}|^{2(N-1)}\chi_{a,N}/(4|r_{a}-1|^{2}): exponential in NN.

The proof is given in App. C.

In this work, we demonstrate that careful preconditioning can mitigate the challenges posed by the ill-conditioned RNN Fisher spectrum, resulting in stable natural-gradient optimization, as discussed in the results section.

III Results

We perform extensive hyperparameter searches for both Adam and minSR. We describe our hyperparameter experiments in App. D. We initialize training using the same initial RNN parameters for both minSR and Adam.

III.1 1D Transverse-Field Ising Model

We benchmark minSR against Adam in finding the ground-state wave function on a variety of models, starting with the simplest case of a one-dimensional stoquastic Hamiltonian, namely the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (TFIM). The Hamiltonian of the 1D TFIM is given by

ℋ^TFIM=−J∑i=1N−1σ^izσ^i+1z−h∑i=1Nσ^ix,\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\textrm{TFIM}}=-J\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{i+1}^{z}-h\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}, (37)

where JJ and hh are coupling constants, and σ^x,y,z\hat{\sigma}^{x,y,z} are the Pauli matrices. We work with open boundary conditions (OBC) and choose J=1=hJ=1=h, which corresponds to the critical point [59]. The stoquasticity of this Hamiltonian [60] allows us to represent the ground state with a pRNN wave function.

For a fair comparison, we evaluate both optimizers over the same training time, allowing Adam to take more steps than minSR. In particular, over the course of a 500500-second training session, we show that using minSR we can achieve several orders of magnitude improvement over the Adam optimizer. In Fig. 2, we plot the performance of both minSR and Adam on the TFIM with N=200N=200 spins. We compare the relative error of both optimizers

Rel.Err.=ERNN−Eref|Eref|,\operatorname{Rel.Err.}=\frac{E_{\textrm{RNN}}-E_{\textrm{ref}}}{|E_{\textrm{ref}}|}, (38)

where ErefE_{\textrm{ref}} is the lowest reference energy available from the literature or the exact result from theory. We obtain this performance using a single fixed value of λ\lambda. The poor conditioning of the SR matrix comes from the structure of the RNN itself. App. C illustrates mechanisms by which recurrent architectures can generate ill-conditioning in a simplified model; this motivates Tikhonov regularization in the GRU experiments, since it makes the minSR preconditioner well conditioned. We further analyze the training instabilities associated with ill-conditioning in App. E. Hyperparameters of our simulation are reported in App. D.

III.2 1D Cluster State

We now turn to the 1D Cluster state benchmark, which corresponds to a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian. The Cluster state is a key model for measurement-based quantum computation [62]. It is known to have long-range conditional mutual information, making it challenging to learn using NQS [62]. The Cluster state corresponds to the ground state of the following Hamiltonian:

ℋ^CS=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\textrm{CS}}= −∑k=2N−2σ^xk−1σ^zkσ^xk+1−σ^z1σ^x2\displaystyle-\sum_{k=2}^{N-2}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{k-1}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{k}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{k+1}-\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{1}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{2}
−σ^N−1x​σ^Nx−σ^N−2x​σ^N−1z​σ^Nz.\displaystyle-\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{N-1}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{N}-\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{N-2}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{N-1}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{N}.

Since this Hamiltonian is non-stoquastic, we use a cRNN wave function as our ansatz. Note that RNN wave functions [62] and Dilated RNN wave functions [52] have already been applied to this problem and only optimized using the Adam optimizer. In Ref. [63], RNN wave functions optimized with Adam achieve a relative error of about 10−210^{-2} with a system size N=64N=64. In Fig. 2(b), we achieve very low errors, far below those of the Adam optimizer. Using minSR on a larger system size of N=100N=100 spins, our final variational energy E=−99.99​(4)E=-99.99(4) is very close to the theoretical value of E=−100E=-100. Here too, minSR is stabilized by a single constant Tikhonov shift λ\lambda, with no schedule; the values used are listed in App. D. Overall, we demonstrate that RNN wave functions implemented with the traditional GRU cell, optimized with minSR, can numerically capture long-range conditional correlations of the Cluster state without the need for advanced RNN models such as Dilated RNNs [52].

III.3 Square Lattice J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Model

We now move our benchmark comparison towards two-dimensional systems. Here we focus on the square lattice J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model given by

ℋ^J1​J2\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{J_{1}J_{2}} =J14​∑⟨i​j⟩(σ^ix​σ^jx+σ^iy​σ^jy+σ^iz​σ^jz)\displaystyle=\frac{J_{1}}{4}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{x}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{y}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{y}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{z}\bigr)
+J24∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩(σ^ixσ^jx+σ^iyσ^jy+σ^izσ^jz),\displaystyle+\frac{J_{2}}{4}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle}\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{x}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{y}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{y}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{z}\bigr),

where σ^x,y,z\hat{\sigma}^{x,y,z} are Pauli operators and J1J_{1}, J2J_{2} are coupling constants, and we set J1=1J_{1}=1. Also note that ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle (⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle) correspond to nearest (next-nearest) neighbours. The two main cases of interest are: J2=0J_{2}=0 corresponding to the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, and J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 corresponding to a frustrated regime. This frustration point is often used to benchmark the strengths and weaknesses of NQS methods [12, 24, 7].

We begin with the unfrustrated point J2=0J_{2}=0, where we use a 2D pRNN wave function as our ansatz. Even though the Hamiltonian is originally non-stoquastic, a simple Marshall sign rotation can be applied to make it stoquastic [64, 65]. Similar to the relative error metric used for the one-dimensional benchmarks, the accuracy of an NQS can also be assessed by using a standard metric, which combines the energy and variance into a single dimensionless parameter known as the V-score [66]:

V-score=N⋅Var⁡[ϵ](E−E∞)2.\textbf{V-score}=\frac{N\cdot\operatorname{Var}[\bm{\epsilon}]}{(E-E_{\infty})^{2}}. (39)

Here NN is the number of spins and E∞E_{\infty} is the infinite-temperature energy, which is equal to zero for this model [66]. This metric eliminates the need for an accurate reference energy while providing the same scaling behavior as the relative error near convergence [66]. In Fig. 3(a), we show that minSR achieves a lower V-score than Adam over the same time period, as well as lower energy and energy variance as reported in Tab. 2. However, we note that the advantage of minSR is less pronounced relative to the previous one-dimensional benchmarks. In our hyperparameter tuning experiments, we choose an increasing value of the Tikhonov regularization parameter, λ=3×10−4⋅‖𝒯‖2/3\lambda=3\times 10^{-4}\cdot\|\mathcal{T}\|^{2/3}, where ‖𝒯‖\|\mathcal{T}\| generally starts with a small value at the start of training, then increases several orders of magnitude and then finally settles at a large value that is usually in the range ‖𝒯‖∼105−8\|\mathcal{T}\|\sim 10^{5-8}. Using this power of 23\frac{2}{3} was empirically found to give superior results for dh=100d_{h}=100 compared to a constant λ\lambda. This can be explained by the model preferring natural gradient updates, which correspond to a small λ\lambda, during the initial period of training and SGD, which corresponds to having a large value of λ\lambda, during the later stages of training.

In the frustrated regime (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5), we apply a Marshall sign rule [64, 65]

Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=(−1)σA​Ψ~𝜽​(𝝈),\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=(-1)^{\sigma_{A}}\tilde{\Psi}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}), (40)

where σA=∑i∈Aσi\sigma_{A}=\sum_{i\in A}\sigma_{i} and the sum over AA runs over every other spin on the square lattice. Here the amplitudes Ψ~𝜽​(𝝈)\tilde{\Psi}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) are modeled by a two-dimensional cRNN wave function. This rule corresponds to the exact sign structure for J2=0J_{2}=0 and can be used to improve NQS performance for relatively small J2J_{2} [14, 13, 10].

For minSR regularization, we use the trust region learning rate η∗\eta_{*} from Eq. (121), which adapts the step-size in both parameter space and in distribution space to be within a trust region (see App. F). In Fig. 3(b), we observe that minSR and Adam have comparable V-scores, though minSR converges slightly faster initially. In particular, the results show significant instability, suffering from strong fluctuations in the V-score throughout training. We find that a constant value of λ=10−1\lambda=10^{-1} provides the best results.

In both unfrustrated and frustrated models, we find training to be very sensitive to the damping scheme. When applying the Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) scheme (described in App. G), we find that λ\lambda tends to diverge as a result of the poor conditioning of the landscape. Because larger λ\lambda corresponds to stronger damping, the observed growth of λ\lambda indicates that the local quadratic model is trusted only over increasingly small parameter displacements, at least with a small number of samples. This can substantially reduce the benefit of the minSR preconditioner. Certain parameters become very sensitive to even small step sizes, making a uniform trust region for all parameter directions a poor choice.

Naive schemes such as using λ×diag​(𝒯)\lambda\times\textrm{diag}(\mathcal{T}) as a preconditioner instead of λ​𝕀\lambda\mathbb{I} can result in very small updates and poor final energies. Structural Damping is a more sophisticated damping scheme that has been successful in second-order RNN optimization [67] by penalizing sudden changes in hidden state trajectories. However, it is too computationally expensive to implement for larger-scale RNNs.

We conjecture that the 2D RNN wave function architecture, inspired by the multi-dimensional RNN (MDRNN) introduced in Ref. [68], may be the cause of the large discrepancy between the performance of natural gradients in 1D and 2D. In one dimension, each cell passes its hidden state to a single neighbor. In two dimensions, each cell receives hidden states from two neighbors. As a result, the number of paths along which gradients travel grows combinatorially with system size, leading to training instabilities [69]. Additionally, in Ref. [70], it is shown that Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) based MDRNNs can face exploding gradients, similarly to 1D Vanilla RNNs. More stable multi-dimensional RNNs have been proposed, such as the GridLSTM [69] or replacing the GRU cell with a Leaky Lowpass (LeakyLP) cell [70]. Designing a more stable 2D RNN architecture may reduce ill-conditioning of the loss landscape, enabling a more efficient natural gradient optimization, without the need for more sophisticated damping schemes.

IV Loss landscape

In the previous section, we observed that minSR was significantly more successful in 1D and hypothesized that the 2D loss landscapes may be ill-conditioned. In this section, we visualize these landscapes along certain parameter directions. In Ref. [71], plotting along two random parameter directions, with appropriate parameter normalization, has been shown to provide useful insights into the geometry of the loss landscape.

We plot the energy E⁡(𝜽∗+x​𝒗max+y​𝒗min)E(\bm{\theta}_{*}+x\bm{v}_{\mathrm{max}}+y\bm{v}_{\min}), where 𝜽∗\bm{\theta}_{*} denotes the optimized variational parameters obtained after training. 𝒗max\bm{v}_{\max} and 𝒗min\bm{v}_{\min} are parameter-space directions corresponding to finite-sample approximations to the eigenvectors of SS with eigenvalues approximating λmax\lambda_{\max} and λmin\lambda_{\min}, respectively. A similar choice of vmaxv_{\max} and vminv_{\min} has been proposed to accurately capture saddle points [72], and it may allow us to focus on ill-conditioned portions of the loss landscape. To ensure our comparison of the different landscapes is not biased by the size of the weights and biases, we ensure ‖𝒗max‖=‖𝒗min‖=‖𝜽∗‖\|\bm{v}_{\max}\|=\|\bm{v}_{\min}\|=\|\bm{\theta}_{*}\| for each of our models [71].

In Fig. 4, we observe that the loss landscape of the 2D Heisenberg model is very ill-conditioned in comparison to the smooth loss landscape in the 1D TFIM model. Its convex region in the center is 10 times smaller in the xx direction. This indicates that the variational energy becomes more sensitive to small changes in certain parameters, reminiscent of other models that face exploding gradients. This observation suggests that using a uniform λ\lambda across all parameter directions may be a suboptimal choice, and that parameter-dependent damping should be introduced.

These plots support the hypothesis that loss-landscape ill-conditioning contributes to minSR’s reduced advantage in two spatial dimensions. More stable architectures or damping schemes may therefore improve optimization in two dimensions.

V Scaling study

In this section, we explore the effect of NsN_{s} on the performance of minSR. We find that accurate variational energies can be obtained even with Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p}. In Fig. 5(a), we plot both the V-score scaling of Adam and minSR with increased NsN_{s}, while holding the hidden dimension constant. All experiments are run for a training time of 24 hours as a control, leading to fewer training iterations for minSR and for larger NsN_{s}. Adam achieves nearly twice as many training iterations as minSR for Ns=150N_{s}=150. Despite this speed advantage, minSR outperforms Adam for all values of NsN_{s}. Additionally, the advantage of minSR over Adam increases with NsN_{s}, while their performance is similar for low sample sizes.

The sensitivity of minSR to NsN_{s} can be explained by the accuracy of our finite-sample SR metric. In particular, a good approximation of the SR metric requires Ns≫NpN_{s}\gg N_{p}, where NpN_{p} is the total number of parameters, e.g., Ns≈10​NpN_{s}\approx 10N_{p}, which is recommended in the literature [39]. Theoretical error bounds for the subsampled SR matrix follow from a Markov inequality argument [73, 74]. We state the result as Proposition 3 and prove it in App. H.

Proposition 3 (Subsampled QGT error bound)

Let the configurations 𝛔(1),…,𝛔(Ns)\bm{\sigma}^{(1)},\dots,\bm{\sigma}^{(N_{s})} be drawn i.i.d. from |Ψ𝛉|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}, which exact autoregressive sampling guarantees, and write

Oi(𝝈)=∂θilogΨ𝜽(𝝈),i=1,…,Np,O_{i}(\bm{\sigma})=\partial_{\theta_{i}}\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}),\qquad i=1,\dots,N_{p},

for the log-derivatives, which may be complex. Define

μi≡𝔼⁡[Oi],Xi≡Oi−μi.\mu_{i}\equiv\mathbb{E}[O_{i}],\qquad X_{i}\equiv O_{i}-\mu_{i}. (41)

Let QQ denote the population QGT, with entries

Qi​j=𝔼⁡[Xi​Xj∗],Q_{ij}=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{j}^{*}], (42)

and let Q~\widetilde{Q} be the corresponding population-centered NsN_{s}-sample estimator,

Q~i​j=1Ns​∑s=1NsXi​(𝝈(s))​Xj​(𝝈(s))∗.\widetilde{Q}_{ij}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s=1}^{N_{s}}X_{i}\big(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}\big)X_{j}\big(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}\big)^{*}. (43)

Then 𝔼⁡[Q~]=Q\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Q}]=Q. Let

Vavg(c)≡1Np2​∑i,j=1NpVar⁡(Xi​Xj∗)V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{p}^{2}}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N_{p}}\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}X_{j}^{*}) (44)

be the average variance of a single-sample matrix element, where Var⁡(Z)≡𝔼⁡[|Z−𝔼⁡[Z]|2]\operatorname{Var}(Z)\equiv\mathbb{E}[|Z-\mathbb{E}[Z]|^{2}], and assume Vavg(c)<∞V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}<\infty. Then, for every ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon,

‖Q−Q~‖F≤NpNs​Vavg(c)ϵ.\|Q-\widetilde{Q}\|_{F}\leq\frac{N_{p}}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\sqrt{\frac{V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}}{\epsilon}}. (45)

For real variational parameters, the population SR metric is S=Re⁡QS=\operatorname{Re}Q. Defining S~=Re⁡Q~\widetilde{S}=\operatorname{Re}\widetilde{Q}, the same bound implies

‖S−S~‖F≤α−1​Vavg(c)ϵ,\|S-\widetilde{S}\|_{F}\leq\alpha^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}}{\epsilon}}, (46)

where α=Ns/Np\alpha=\sqrt{N_{s}}/N_{p}. The same right-hand side also bounds the corresponding spectral norms, since ‖A‖2≤‖A‖F\|A\|_{2}\leq\|A\|_{F}.

The proof is provided in App. H. Note that computing S~\widetilde{S} with an empirical mean μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i}, as we do in our numerical simulations, still results in an upper bound proportional to α−1\alpha^{-1} as highlighted in App. H.

In Fig. 5(b), we plot the relative error between the subsampled Fisher S~\tilde{S} and a high-sample reference estimate SS of the Fisher matrix for the two-dimensional J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model. We use Ns≳NpN_{s}\gtrsim N_{p} to construct this reference Fisher estimate. We observe that as α\alpha grows, the decay rate of the subsampling error qualitatively matches the inverse relationship with α\alpha theoretically predicted by the upper bound (46).

VI Conclusions

In this work, we demonstrate a stable and reproducible application of minSR for optimizing RNN wave functions within the VMC framework. Our methodology is based on the standard regularization of the Fisher matrix. Our results show a significant improvement over the Adam optimizer on the 1D TFIM and 1D cluster state benchmarks. In contrast, we obtain comparable performance to the Adam optimizer in two spatial dimensions, namely on the square lattice Heisenberg and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model benchmarks. In most of our experiments, we observe faster convergence of the minSR setup compared to the first-order optimizer using only a few hundred Monte Carlo samples. Our scaling study further shows that a subsampled SR matrix with Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p} remains a useful preconditioner, with an estimation error consistent with the theoretical bound in Eq. (46).

An important investigation path for future work is to check whether the combinatorial growth of backpropagation paths in the two-dimensional RNN architecture is the main cause behind the ill-conditioned loss landscape [69]. More sophisticated damping techniques may enable minSR to optimize on ill-conditioned loss landscapes. Alternatively, GridLSTM cells are known to overcome this ill-conditioning and merit further exploration [69]. Additionally, the LeakyLP [70] cell could yield a two-dimensional RNN wave function that delivers superior results under minSR optimization. Our results also highlight the memory advantage provided by first-order optimizers, which allow for scalability to very large system sizes [21]. Deploying second-order optimization on small system sizes for faster convergence, and then switching to first-order optimizers on large system sizes under an iterative training procedure [16, 14, 18, 19, 21], offers a practical route to balancing accuracy and scalability against the memory limits of available hardware. Additionally, we note that our variational energies are calculated without applying point group symmetries on our RNN ansatz, as our main goal is to compare minSR and Adam optimizers on equal footing. We believe that imposing physical symmetries on our architecture will further improve our variational accuracies through large-scale simulations, which we plan to pursue in future work.

An open question raised by our results is whether the geometry of the variational manifold can predict when minSR outperforms first-order optimizers. In particular, the spectrum of the QGT and the effective dimension of the sample-spanned tangent space may quantify how much curvature information is captured by a finite number of samples. Relating these information-geometric quantities to the observed performance gap between minSR and Adam across models and spatial dimensions is therefore a promising direction for future work [43]. More broadly, geometric and curvature-aware methods have proved useful for characterizing and improving learning dynamics in other machine-learning settings [75, 76, 77], suggesting that a similar systematic study of variational geometry could provide useful diagnostics for predicting optimization performance in neural quantum states.
