Appendix A Gated Recurrent Unit Cells

To mitigate the vanishing gradient problem present in Vanilla RNNs, GRUs introduce three additional vectors 𝒉~i,𝒓i,𝒖i\tilde{\bm{h}}_{i},\bm{r}_{i},\bm{u}_{i} to capture memory in addition to the hidden state 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i}. Here we present the GRU architecture introduced in Ref. [78]. Its recursion update rules are as follows:

𝒖i\displaystyle\bm{u}_{i} =Sigmoid⁡(Wu​[𝒉i−1;𝝈i−1]+𝒃u),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sigmoid}(W_{u}[\bm{h}_{i-1};\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}]+\bm{b}_{u}), (47)
𝒓i\displaystyle\bm{r}_{i} =Sigmoid⁡(Wr​[𝒉i−1;𝝈i−1]+𝒃r),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sigmoid}(W_{r}[\bm{h}_{i-1};\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}]+\bm{b}_{r}), (48)
𝒉~i\displaystyle\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i} =tanh⁡(𝒓i⊙(Wh​𝒉i−1+𝒃h)+Win​𝝈i−1+𝒃in),\displaystyle=\tanh\left(\bm{r}_{i}\odot(W_{\rm h}\bm{h}_{i-1}+\bm{b}_{\rm h})+W_{\rm in}\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}+\bm{b}_{\rm in}\right), (49)
𝒉i\displaystyle\bm{h}_{i} =(1−𝒖i)⊙𝒉i−1+𝒖i⊙𝒉~i.\displaystyle=(1-\bm{u}_{i})\odot\bm{h}_{i-1}+\bm{u}_{i}\odot\tilde{\bm{h}}_{i}. (50)

Here ⊙\odot is the Hadamard product, which multiplies two vectors element-wise. The hidden state 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} is updated based on the interpolation of the previous hidden state 𝒉i−1\bm{h}_{i-1} and the candidate hidden state 𝒉~i\tilde{\bm{h}}_{i}. The update gate 𝒖i\bm{u}_{i} controls this interpolation based on the importance value of 𝝈i−1\bm{\sigma}_{i-1}. The reset gate 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} modifies the candidate hidden state 𝒉~i\tilde{\bm{h}}_{i} by setting certain components of 𝒉i−1\bm{h}_{i-1} to zero when the corresponding components of 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} are close to zero. The reset gate allows the GRU to ‘forget’ irrelevant information, which helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem.

The two-dimensional version of the GRU wave function is implemented as follows:

𝒖i,j\displaystyle\bm{u}_{i,j} =Sigmoid⁡(Wu​[𝒉i,j′;𝝈i,j′]+𝒃u),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sigmoid}(W_{u}[\bm{h}^{\prime}_{i,j};\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}_{i,j}]+\bm{b}_{u}), (51)
𝒓i,j\displaystyle\bm{r}_{i,j} =Sigmoid⁡(Wr​[𝒉i,j′;𝝈i,j′]+𝒃r),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sigmoid}(W_{r}[\bm{h}^{\prime}_{i,j};\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}_{i,j}]+\bm{b}_{r}), (52)
𝒉~i,j\displaystyle\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i,j} =tanh⁡(𝒓i,j⊙(Wh​𝒉i,j′+𝒃h)+Win​𝝈i,j′+𝒃in),\displaystyle=\tanh\left(\bm{r}_{i,j}\odot(W_{\rm h}\bm{h}^{\prime}_{i,j}+\bm{b}_{\rm h})+W_{\rm in}\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}_{i,j}+\bm{b}_{\rm in}\right), (53)
𝒉i,j\displaystyle\bm{h}_{i,j} =(1−𝒖i,j)⊙𝒉i,j′+𝒖i,j⊙𝒉~i,j,\displaystyle=(1-\bm{u}_{i,j})\odot\bm{h}^{\prime}_{i,j}+\bm{u}_{i,j}\odot\tilde{\bm{h}}_{i,j}{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25},} (54)

where

𝒉i,j′\displaystyle\bm{h}^{\prime}_{i,j} =U1​𝒉i−(−1)j,j+U2​𝒉i,j−1,\displaystyle=U_{1}\bm{h}_{i-(-1)^{j},j}+U_{2}\bm{h}_{i,j-1}, (55)
𝝈i,j′\displaystyle\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}_{i,j} =[𝝈i−(−1)j,j;𝝈i,j−1].\displaystyle=[\bm{\sigma}_{i-(-1)^{j},j};\bm{\sigma}_{i,j-1}]. (56)

Here U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} are additional trainable weights.

Appendix B minSR with Momentum

We add momentum to our minSR scheme, which has previously been observed to increase performance in SR [79]. We can write our SR parameter updates as 𝜽t+1=𝜽t−δ​𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\delta\bm{\theta}_{t}. The corresponding momentum-based parameter update is given by

𝒎t+1\displaystyle\bm{m}_{t+1} =μ​𝒎t+(1−μ)​δ​𝜽t,\displaystyle=\mu\bm{m}_{t}+(1-\mu)\delta\bm{\theta}_{t}, (57)
𝜽t+1\displaystyle\bm{\theta}_{t+1} =𝜽t−𝒎t+1.\displaystyle=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bm{m}_{t+1}.

Here μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) is the momentum hyperparameter, with μ=0\mu=0 corresponding to regular SGD. 𝒎\bm{m} is the momentum vector which stores the previous history of updates. We present the momentum values for training in App. D. We attempted using the SPRING algorithm [79], and found that it performs slightly worse than minSR.

Appendix C Derivation of stochastic-reconfiguration ill-conditioning in RNN wave functions

The SR matrix S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} of an autoregressive RNN wave function is ill-conditioned from both ends of its spectrum, with exact gauge zero modes at the bottom and recurrently amplified modes scaling as N3N^{3} (marginal) or exponentially in NN (expanding) at the top. This appendix proves Proposition 1 and Proposition 2, stated in Sec. II.5 of the main text. Subsection C.1 fixes the model and exhibits its hidden-coordinate gauge map. Subsection C.2 proves Proposition 1. Subsections C.3 and C.4 rewrite the SR matrix SS in terms of the logits 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} rather than the raw network parameters. This logit-coordinate form is the starting point for the eigenvalue bounds proved in Subsections C.5 and C.6. Subsections C.5 and C.6 prove Proposition 2. The derivation is deliberately granular: each hypothesis is made explicit at the step where it is used.

C.1 Setup and hidden-coordinate gauge freedom

We first fix the model and exhibit its parametrization redundancy. The intuition is geometric: the RNN cell communicates with the outputs only through the logits, so any change of the internal hidden coordinates that the logits cannot see is physically invisible and must leave the state invariant.

We work with a real, positive, autoregressive wave function whose Born probability factorizes over sites,

|Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)|2=P𝜽​(𝝈)=∏i=1Np𝜽​(σi|σ<i),|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}=P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i}), (58)

where 𝝈=(σ1,…,σN)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{N}) is a spin configuration, σ<i=(σ1,…,σi−1)\sigma_{<i}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{i-1}) is its history, and 𝜽\bm{\theta} collects all variational parameters. As we assume Ψ𝜽>0\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}>0, taking the logarithm of Eq. (58) and using log⁡Ψ=12​log⁡P\log\Psi=\tfrac{1}{2}\log P gives

log⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=12​log⁡P𝜽​(𝝈)=12​∑i=1Nlog⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i),\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\frac{1}{2}\log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i}), (59)

where the second equality is the logarithm of the product in Eq. (58).

The conditionals are produced by a linear recurrent cell. At site ii the hidden state 𝐡i∈ℝdh\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} and logit vector 𝐳i∈ℝq\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} are

𝐡i=W​𝐡i−1+V​𝝈i+𝐛,𝐳i=U​𝐡i−1+𝐜,\mathbf{h}_{i}=W\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+V\bm{\sigma}_{i}+\mathbf{b},\qquad\mathbf{z}_{i}=U\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+\mathbf{c}, (60)

where 𝝈i∈ℝdσ\bm{\sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} is the one-hot encoding of the local spin σi\sigma_{i} over its dσd_{\sigma} possible values, W∈ℝdh×dhW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{h}} is the recurrent matrix, V∈ℝdh×dσV\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{\sigma}} the input matrix, U∈ℝdσ×dhU\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}\times d_{h}} the readout matrix, and 𝐛∈ℝdh\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}, 𝐜∈ℝdσ\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\sigma}} the biases. Throughout, we take the standing convention that the initial hidden state is fixed at 𝐡0=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}; this both gives the recursion a starting point and, as we use below, makes it invariant under the hidden-coordinate map. The conditional distribution is the softmax of the logits,

𝐩i=softmax⁡(𝐳i),p𝜽​(σi|σ<i)=𝐩i𝖳​𝝈i,\mathbf{p}_{i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{i}),\qquad p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i})=\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{\sigma}_{i}, (61)

where the last equality selects the component of 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} indexed by the realized one-hot 𝝈i\bm{\sigma}_{i}.

This parametrization carries a continuous hidden-coordinate gauge symmetry. For any invertible A∈G​L​(dh)A\in GL(d_{h}), apply the change of internal basis 𝐡i↦A​𝐡i\mathbf{h}_{i}\mapsto A\mathbf{h}_{i} (consistently for all i≥0i\geq 0, so that in particular 𝐡0=𝟎↦A​𝟎=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}\mapsto A\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}) together with

W↦AWA−1,V↦AV,𝐛↦A𝐛,U↦UA−1,𝐜↦𝐜.\begin{gathered}W\mapsto AWA^{-1},\qquad V\mapsto AV,\qquad\mathbf{b}\mapsto A\mathbf{b},\\[2.0pt] U\mapsto UA^{-1},\qquad\mathbf{c}\mapsto\mathbf{c}.\end{gathered} (62)

We check by induction on ii that the recursion in Eq. (60) maps 𝐡i↦A​𝐡i\mathbf{h}_{i}\mapsto A\mathbf{h}_{i}. Base case i=0i=0. The fixed initial state obeys 𝐡0=𝟎↦A​𝟎=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}\mapsto A\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}, so the claim holds trivially. This is where the choice 𝐡0=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0} is needed. Inductive step. Assume 𝐡i−1↦A​𝐡i−1\mathbf{h}_{i-1}\mapsto A\mathbf{h}_{i-1}. Substituting the transformed quantities into the hidden update gives

𝐡i′\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime} =(A​W​A−1)​(A​𝐡i−1)+(A​V)​𝝈i+A​𝐛\displaystyle=(AWA^{-1})(A\mathbf{h}_{i-1})+(AV)\bm{\sigma}_{i}+A\mathbf{b}
=A⁡(W​𝐡i−1+V​𝝈i+𝐛)=A​𝐡i,\displaystyle=A\big(W\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+V\bm{\sigma}_{i}+\mathbf{b}\big)=A\mathbf{h}_{i}, (63)

where the first line inserts the maps of Eq. (62) together with the induction hypothesis. The second line uses A−1​A=𝕀A^{-1}A=\mathbb{I} and factors out AA, which closes the induction. The logits are then strictly unchanged (invariant) because A−1​A=𝕀A^{-1}A=\mathbb{I} cancels the change of internal basis.

𝐳i↦(U​A−1)​(A​𝐡i−1)+𝐜=U​𝐡i−1+𝐜=𝐳i.\mathbf{z}_{i}\mapsto(UA^{-1})(A\mathbf{h}_{i-1})+\mathbf{c}=U\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{z}_{i}. (64)

The invariance now propagates forward. First, the softmax output 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} of Eq. (61) is unchanged, since it sees the parameters only through 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i}. Second, so is the product P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}} of Eq. (58), and hence Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}} itself. Moving along the orbit generated by A∈G​L​(dh)A\in GL(d_{h}) therefore changes the parameters but leaves the physical state identical.

C.2 Exact Fisher zero modes from the gauge orbit

Proof of Proposition 1. The gauge orbit has infinitesimal generators: the directions in which the parameters move when the change of basis is first switched on. We now show that these are exact zero modes of SS, not simply approximate ones. Along these directions the log-amplitude does not move for any single configuration, so the log-derivative vector that builds SS vanishes identically.

So far we have considered a finite change of basis AA. To identify directions in parameter space we need infinitesimal ones, so we take AA to be a small departure from doing nothing,

A=𝕀+t​X,A=\mathbb{I}+t\,X, (65)

where XX is an arbitrary fixed dh×dhd_{h}\times d_{h} matrix that selects which change of basis we perform, and the small number tt controls its size. Setting t=0t=0 gives A=𝕀A=\mathbb{I}, i.e. no change at all.

As tt varies, Eq. (62) turns this into a smooth path 𝜽⁡(t)\bm{\theta}(t) through parameter space. Every point on this path describes the same wave function, since each value of tt corresponds to a valid change of basis.

To find the explicit components of d​𝜽d\bm{\theta}, we substitute A=𝕀+t​XA=\mathbb{I}+tX into the transformation rules of Eq. (62) and keep only the terms proportional to tt. We also need the inverse to the same order,

A−1=𝕀−t​X+𝒪⁡(t2),A^{-1}=\mathbb{I}-tX+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}), (66)

which follows from (𝕀+t​X)​(𝕀−t​X)=𝕀−t2​X2=𝕀+𝒪⁡(t2)(\mathbb{I}+tX)(\mathbb{I}-tX)=\mathbb{I}-t^{2}X^{2}=\mathbb{I}+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}).

Take the recurrent matrix as a worked example:

W↦A​W​A−1\displaystyle W\;\mapsto\;AWA^{-1} =(𝕀+t​X)​W​(𝕀−t​X)+𝒪⁡(t2)\displaystyle=(\mathbb{I}+tX)\,W\,(\mathbb{I}-tX)+\mathcal{O}(t^{2})
=W+t⁡(X​W−W​X)+𝒪⁡(t2).\displaystyle=W+t\,(XW-WX)+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}). (67)

The two terms carry opposite signs, one coming from each side of WW. Their difference is the commutator of XX and WW,

[X,W]≡X​W−W​X,[X,W]\equiv XW-WX, (68)

also known as the Lie bracket. It measures the extent to which two matrices fail to commute, and vanishes precisely when X​W=W​XXW=WX.

The commutator appears only for WW. The reason is that WW is the only matrix that takes a hidden state and returns another hidden state, so both of its sides feel the change of basis: AA multiplies it from the left and A−1A^{-1} from the right, W↦A​W​A−1W\mapsto AWA^{-1}. Each side then contributes one term, and the two carry opposite signs, so their difference is taken. Every other parameter meets the hidden space on one side only, for example V↦A​VV\mapsto AV, so it contributes a single term and no difference is formed. Repeating the same substitution for each remaining parameter gives

dW=[X,W]t,dV=XVt,d𝐛=X𝐛t,dU=−UXt,d𝐜=𝟎.\begin{gathered}dW=[X,W]t,\qquad dV=XVt,\qquad d\mathbf{b}=X\mathbf{b}t,\\[2.0pt] dU=-UXt,\qquad d\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}.\end{gathered} (69)

Note that d​𝐜=𝟎d\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0} because 𝐜\mathbf{c} never appears with an AA at all.

These are our candidate zero directions, and we can indeed confirm them immediately. Eq. (64) showed that the logits are exactly unchanged for every AA, hence for every value of tt. A quantity that never changes has zero rate of change, so

d​𝐳i=𝟎for all ​i,d\mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathbf{0}\qquad\text{for all }i, (70)

since 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} is constant along the whole orbit. Because log⁡Ψ𝜽\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}} depends on 𝜽\bm{\theta} only through the logits {𝐳i}\{\mathbf{z}_{i}\} (Eqs. (59)–(61)), the chain rule and Eq. (70) yield

d​log⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=∑i=1N∂log⁡Ψ𝜽∂𝐳i⋅d​𝐳i=0for every ​𝝈.d\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\partial\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}{\partial\mathbf{z}_{i}}\!\cdot d\mathbf{z}_{i}=0\qquad\text{for every }\bm{\sigma}. (71)

We now feed this result into SS. Recall from the main text how SS is assembled from a sample of NsN_{s} configurations 𝝈(1),…,𝝈(Ns)\bm{\sigma}^{(1)},\dots,\bm{\sigma}^{(N_{s})}. The (unnormalized) log-derivative matrix has entries

𝒪k​s=1Ns​∂θklog⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈(s)),\mathcal{O}_{ks}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\,\partial_{\theta_{k}}\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}), (72)

where kk labels the parameter and ss labels the sample. Subtracting from each row its own sample mean gives the centered matrix 𝒪¯\bar{\mathcal{O}},

𝒪¯k​s=𝒪k​s−1Ns​∑s′𝒪k​s′,\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ks}=\mathcal{O}_{ks}-\tfrac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s^{\prime}}\mathcal{O}_{ks^{\prime}}, (73)

and S=Q=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=Q=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} for real-valued wavefunctions. To test whether a gauge direction d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} is a zero mode, we evaluate the quadratic form d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}, that is, we contract SS with d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} on both of its indices, multiplying it by d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} on the left and on the right,

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽=‖𝒪¯†​d​𝜽‖22=∑s=1Ns|(𝒪¯†​d​𝜽)s|2,d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}=\big\|\,\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}d\bm{\theta}\,\big\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{s=1}^{N_{s}}\Big|\big(\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}d\bm{\theta}\big)_{s}\Big|^{2}, (74)

where the first equality writes the quadratic form as a norm using S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}. Each entry (𝒪¯†​d​𝜽)s\big(\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}d\bm{\theta}\big)_{s} is the centered directional log-derivative 1Ns​(d​log⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈(s))−d​log⁡Ψ¯)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\big(d\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)})-\overline{d\log\Psi}\,\big), which vanishes because Eq. (71) holds configuration by configuration. Hence

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽=0,d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}=0, (75)

for any sample. Nothing in the argument required many samples, since each square vanished on its own. The gauge directions are therefore exact zero modes of SS in two senses. First, in the infinite-sample limit. Second, for every finite-sample estimate 𝒪¯​𝒪¯†\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}. These are the Fisher-information singularities: null directions of SS along which the parameters change but the wave function does not. It remains to show that d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} lies in ker⁡S\ker S, in both the finite-sample and the population case. For a finite sample, Eq. (74) makes every entry of 𝒪¯†​d​𝜽\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}d\bm{\theta} vanish, so S​d​𝜽=𝒪¯​(𝒪¯†​d​𝜽)=𝟎S\,d\bm{\theta}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\big(\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}d\bm{\theta}\big)=\mathbf{0}. For the population matrix, SS is positive semidefinite, and its quadratic form vanishes along d​𝜽d\bm{\theta}; since a positive semidefinite matrix annihilates any vector on which its quadratic form is zero, S​d​𝜽=𝟎S\,d\bm{\theta}=\mathbf{0} there too. The generator XX was arbitrary, so every gauge direction lies in ker⁡S\ker S: the tangent space of the G​L​(dh)GL(d_{h}) gauge orbit is contained in ker⁡S\ker S. □\square

C.3 The Fisher quadratic form in logit coordinates

In these two subsections, we derive the logit-coordinate form of the population SR matrix, Eq. (97), which the proof of Proposition 2 (Secs. C.5 and C.6) takes as its starting point. Having established that the gauge directions are exact zero modes, we now turn to the remaining directions. We express the Fisher form in logit coordinates, where its structure is most transparent. The autoregressive factorization then reduces it to a sum of per-site contributions: the cross terms between different sites vanish because the score of each conditional distribution has zero mean.

It is easier to compute the Fisher form of the probability distribution first and convert to the wave function at the end. We therefore define the classical Fisher quadratic form,

𝒮P​(d​𝜽,d​𝜽)=⟨[d​log⁡P𝜽​(𝝈)]2⟩,\mathcal{S}_{P}(d\bm{\theta},d\bm{\theta})=\Big\langle\big[d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\big]^{2}\Big\rangle, (76)

where ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle denotes the expectation over configurations 𝝈\bm{\sigma} drawn from P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}}, and d​log⁡P𝜽d\log P_{\bm{\theta}} is the change in log⁡P𝜽\log P_{\bm{\theta}} produced by the parameter displacement d​𝜽d\bm{\theta}. It is a quadratic form because d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} enters twice, through the square; both arguments are therefore written out. It is classical because it is built from the probability distribution P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}} rather than from the amplitude Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}.

To evaluate it we need d​log⁡P𝜽d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}. Multiplying Eq. (59) by two removes the factor of 1/21/2 and leaves

log⁡P𝜽​(𝝈)=∑i=1Nlog⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i),\log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i}), (77)

and differentiating this sum term by term gives

d​log⁡P𝜽​(𝝈)=∑i=1Nd​log⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i),d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i}), (78)

To build 𝒮P\mathcal{S}_{P} we must square this sum. It is convenient to abbreviate the site-ii score as

ui≡d​log⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i),u_{i}\equiv d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i}), (79)

so that d​log⁡P𝜽=∑iuid\log P_{\bm{\theta}}=\sum_{i}u_{i}. The square of a sum is a double sum,

[∑i=1Nui]2=∑i=1N∑j=1Nui​uj,\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}\Big]^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}u_{i}u_{j}, (80)

and taking the expectation term by term gives

𝒮P=∑i,j=1N⟨ui​uj⟩,\mathcal{S}_{P}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\big\langle u_{i}u_{j}\big\rangle, (81)

which contains diagonal terms (i=ji=j) and cross terms (i≠ji\neq j). We now show that every cross term vanishes, leaving only the diagonal.

Consider a cross term with i<ji<j. The key observation is that uiu_{i} depends only on the sites σ1,…,σi\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{i}. Since i<ji<j, every one of those sites already belongs to the history σ<j=(σ1,…,σj−1)\sigma_{<j}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{j-1}). Once that history is known, uiu_{i} is therefore a fixed number, not a random one.

This lets us average in two stages: first over σj\sigma_{j} with the history held fixed, then over the history itself. This regrouping is the law of total expectation,

⟨ui​uj⟩=⟨⟨ui​uj|σ<j⟩⟩.\big\langle u_{i}u_{j}\big\rangle=\Big\langle\big\langle u_{i}u_{j}\,\big|\,\sigma_{<j}\big\rangle\Big\rangle. (82)

In the inner average, the history is fixed, so uiu_{i} is a constant and can be taken outside it,

⟨ui​uj⟩=⟨ui​⟨uj|σ<j⟩⟩.\big\langle u_{i}u_{j}\big\rangle=\Big\langle u_{i}\,\big\langle u_{j}\,\big|\,\sigma_{<j}\big\rangle\Big\rangle. (83)

Everything now depends on the inner conditional average ⟨uj|σ<j⟩\langle u_{j}\,|\,\sigma_{<j}\rangle, which vanishes because probabilities are normalized,

⟨d​log⁡p𝜽​(σj|σ<j)|σ<j⟩\displaystyle\big\langle d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{j}|\sigma_{<j})\,\big|\,\sigma_{<j}\big\rangle =∑σjp𝜽​(σj|σ<j)​d​log⁡p𝜽​(σj|σ<j)\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma_{j}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{j}|\sigma_{<j})\,d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{j}|\sigma_{<j})
=∑σjd​p𝜽​(σj|σ<j)\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma_{j}}d\,p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{j}|\sigma_{<j})
=d​∑σjp𝜽​(σj|σ<j)\displaystyle=d\!\sum_{\sigma_{j}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{j}|\sigma_{<j})
=d⁡(1)=0,\displaystyle=d(1)=0, (84)

Here the first line is the definition of the conditional average; the second uses the identity p​d​log⁡p=d​pp\,d\log p=dp; the third interchanges the differential and the finite sum over σj\sigma_{j}; and the last uses the fact that these conditional probabilities sum to one for every history, so that their differential vanishes.

Substituting Eq. (84) into Eq. (83) shows that every term with i<ji<j vanishes. The case i>ji>j follows immediately: the summand in Eq. (81) is symmetric under i↔ji\leftrightarrow j, so exchanging the two indices reduces it to the case just treated. Every off-diagonal term therefore vanishes, and only the diagonal survives,

𝒮P​(d​𝜽,d​𝜽)=∑i=1N⟨[d​log⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i)]2⟩.\mathcal{S}_{P}(d\bm{\theta},d\bm{\theta})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big\langle\big[d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i})\big]^{2}\Big\rangle. (85)

C.4 Softmax covariance

We now evaluate each per-site term of Eq. (85) and connect the classical Fisher form to the wave function SR matrix. Two facts do the work. First, the softmax score is a linear map of the logit displacement, so its second moment is the covariance of the one-hot variable. Second, the amplitude carries a factor 12\tfrac{1}{2} relative to the probability, and squaring turns that 12\tfrac{1}{2} into a 14\tfrac{1}{4}.

We first derive the softmax score explicitly. Here 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} is the logit vector at site ii, 𝐩i=softmax⁡(𝐳i)\mathbf{p}_{i}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{i}) is the conditional probability vector, and 𝝈i\bm{\sigma}_{i} is the one-hot encoding of the realized spin σi\sigma_{i}. For that realized one-hot, Eq. (61) reads

p𝜽​(σi|σ<i)=𝐩i𝖳​𝝈i=ezi,σi∑kezi,k,p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i})=\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{\sigma}_{i}=\frac{e^{z_{i,\sigma_{i}}}}{\sum_{k}e^{z_{i,k}}}, (86)

and taking its logarithm gives

logp𝜽(σi|σ<i)=𝐳i𝖳𝝈i−log∑kezi,k,\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i})=\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\log\!\sum_{k}e^{z_{i,k}}, (87)

where the first term is the selected logit and the second is the log-partition function. Differentiating the log-partition term with respect to the logits,

d​log​∑kezi,k=∑kezi,k​d​zi,k∑k′ezi,k′=∑kpi,k​d​zi,k=𝐩i𝖳​d​𝐳i,d\log\!\sum_{k}e^{z_{i,k}}=\frac{\sum_{k}e^{z_{i,k}}\,dz_{i,k}}{\sum_{k^{\prime}}e^{z_{i,k^{\prime}}}}=\sum_{k}p_{i,k}\,dz_{i,k}=\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}d\mathbf{z}_{i}, (88)

which uses the softmax normalization pi,k=ezi,k/∑k′ezi,k′p_{i,k}=e^{z_{i,k}}/\sum_{k^{\prime}}e^{z_{i,k^{\prime}}}. Now differentiate the first term of Eq. (87). Once σi\sigma_{i} is realized, 𝝈i\bm{\sigma}_{i} is a fixed vector, not a random one, so d⁡(𝐳i𝖳​𝝈i)=𝝈i𝖳​d​𝐳id(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{\sigma}_{i})=\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}d\mathbf{z}_{i}. Subtracting Eq. (88) from this gives the score,

d​log⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i)=(𝝈i−𝐩i)𝖳​d​𝐳i,d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}\,|\,\sigma_{<i})=(\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\mathbf{p}_{i})^{\mathsf{T}}\,d\mathbf{z}_{i}, (89)

where 𝝈i\bm{\sigma}_{i} is the realized one-hot and 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} its mean. Squaring and taking the conditional expectation over σi\sigma_{i} at fixed history σ<i\sigma_{<i} (so that 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} and d​𝐳id\mathbf{z}_{i} are fixed),

⟨[d​log⁡p𝜽​(σi|σ<i)]2|σ<i⟩\displaystyle\Big\langle\big[d\log p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i}|\sigma_{<i})\big]^{2}\,\big|\,\sigma_{<i}\Big\rangle
=d​𝐳i𝖳​⟨(𝝈i−𝐩i)​(𝝈i−𝐩i)𝖳|σ<i⟩​d​𝐳i\displaystyle\quad=d\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\Big\langle(\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\mathbf{p}_{i})(\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\mathbf{p}_{i})^{\mathsf{T}}\,\Big|\,\sigma_{<i}\Big\rangle d\mathbf{z}_{i}
=d​𝐳i𝖳​Ci​d​𝐳i,\displaystyle\quad=d\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\,C_{i}\,d\mathbf{z}_{i}, (90)

where the first line pulls the deterministic d​𝐳id\mathbf{z}_{i} out of the expectation, and the second identifies the conditional covariance CiC_{i} of the one-hot variable. To evaluate CiC_{i}, expand the outer product and use linearity of the conditional expectation,

Ci\displaystyle C_{i} =⟨(𝝈i−𝐩i)​(𝝈i−𝐩i)𝖳|σ<i⟩\displaystyle=\big\langle(\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\mathbf{p}_{i})(\bm{\sigma}_{i}-\mathbf{p}_{i})^{\mathsf{T}}\,\big|\,\sigma_{<i}\big\rangle
=⟨𝝈i​𝝈i𝖳⟩−⟨𝝈i⟩​𝐩i𝖳−𝐩i​⟨𝝈i⟩𝖳+𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳\displaystyle=\big\langle\bm{\sigma}_{i}\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\big\rangle-\big\langle\bm{\sigma}_{i}\big\rangle\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}-\mathbf{p}_{i}\big\langle\bm{\sigma}_{i}\big\rangle^{\mathsf{T}}+\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}
=diag⁡(𝐩i)−𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳−𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳+𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳\displaystyle=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{p}_{i})-\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}-\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}+\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}
=diag⁡(𝐩i)−𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳,\displaystyle=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{p}_{i})-\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}, (91)

where the conditioning on σ<i\sigma_{<i} is left implicit inside ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle. The third line uses two properties of a one-hot vector. First, its outer product with itself is the diagonal matrix built from its own entries, 𝝈i​𝝈i𝖳=diag⁡(𝝈i)\bm{\sigma}_{i}\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}=\operatorname{diag}(\bm{\sigma}_{i}), so averaging gives ⟨𝝈i​𝝈i𝖳⟩=diag⁡(𝐩i)\langle\bm{\sigma}_{i}\bm{\sigma}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\rangle=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{p}_{i}). Second, its mean is the softmax vector itself, ⟨𝝈i⟩=𝐩i\langle\bm{\sigma}_{i}\rangle=\mathbf{p}_{i}. The resulting matrix CiC_{i} is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and is the Fisher matrix of the softmax logits.

Two steps connect 𝒮P\mathcal{S}_{P} to the wave function SR matrix S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}. The first is the relation log⁡Ψ𝜽=12​log⁡P𝜽\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\log P_{\bm{\theta}} between the amplitude and the probability: differentiating and then squaring converts the factor 12\tfrac{1}{2} into 14\tfrac{1}{4},

d​log⁡Ψ=12​d​log⁡P,(d​log⁡Ψ)2=14​(d​log⁡P)2.\begin{gathered}d\log\Psi=\tfrac{1}{2}\,d\log P,\\[2.0pt] (d\log\Psi)^{2}=\tfrac{1}{4}(d\log P)^{2}.\end{gathered} (92)

Second, the total score has zero mean,

⟨d​log⁡P𝜽⟩\displaystyle\big\langle d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}\big\rangle =∑𝝈P𝜽​(𝝈)​d​log⁡P𝜽​(𝝈)\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\,d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})
=d​∑𝝈P𝜽​(𝝈)=d⁡(1)=0,\displaystyle=d\!\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=d(1)=0, (93)

by the same normalization argument as Eq. (84) applied to the joint distribution.

The matrix S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} is built from a finite sample and from centered log-derivatives. The quadratic form it defines is therefore a sample variance,

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽=1Ns​∑s=1Ns(d​log⁡Ψ⁡(𝝈(s))−d​log⁡Ψ¯)2,d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s=1}^{N_{s}}\Big(d\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)})-\overline{d\log\Psi}\Big)^{2}, (94)

where d​log⁡Ψ​(𝝈(s))d\log\Psi(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}) is the change in log⁡Ψ\log\Psi along d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} at sample ss, and d​log⁡Ψ¯\overline{d\log\Psi} is its average over the NsN_{s} samples.

Two things happen as Ns→∞N_{s}\to\infty. First, the sample average converges to the population expectation, so 1Ns​∑s(⋅)→⟨⋅⟩\tfrac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s}(\cdot)\to\langle\cdot\rangle. Second, the subtracted mean vanishes,

d​log⁡Ψ¯⟶⟨d​log⁡Ψ⟩=12​⟨d​log⁡P𝜽⟩=0,\overline{d\log\Psi}\;\longrightarrow\;\langle d\log\Psi\rangle=\tfrac{1}{2}\big\langle d\log P_{\bm{\theta}}\big\rangle=0, (95)

by Eq. (93). The centering therefore drops out, and the quadratic form reduces to

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽\displaystyle d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta} →Ns→∞⟨(d​log⁡Ψ𝜽)2⟩\displaystyle\;\xrightarrow[N_{s}\to\infty]{}\;\big\langle(d\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}})^{2}\big\rangle
=14​⟨(d​log⁡P𝜽)2⟩=14​𝒮P​(d​𝜽,d​𝜽),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\,\big\langle(d\log P_{\bm{\theta}})^{2}\big\rangle=\frac{1}{4}\,\mathcal{S}_{P}(d\bm{\theta},d\bm{\theta}), (96)

where the first arrow uses the two limits just described (centering removed via Eq. (93)), and the second equality uses (d​log⁡Ψ)2=14​(d​log⁡P)2(d\log\Psi)^{2}=\tfrac{1}{4}(d\log P)^{2}. Inserting Eqs. (85) and (90) (and averaging the conditional result over histories) gives the logit-space form of the population SR matrix,

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽=14​∑i=1N⟨d​𝐳i𝖳​Ci​d​𝐳i⟩.d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\langle d\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{i}\,d\mathbf{z}_{i}\big\rangle. (97)

Introducing the logit Jacobian Ji≡∂𝐳i/∂𝜽J_{i}\equiv\partial\mathbf{z}_{i}/\partial\bm{\theta}, so that d​𝐳i=Ji​d​𝜽d\mathbf{z}_{i}=J_{i}\,d\bm{\theta}, and stripping the arbitrary displacement d​𝜽d\bm{\theta} from both sides,

S=14​∑i=1N⟨Ji𝖳​Ci​Ji⟩.S=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\langle J_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{i}J_{i}\big\rangle. (98)

Eq. (97) makes both ends of the spectrum visible. Gauge directions leave the logits unchanged, d​𝐳i=𝟎d\mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathbf{0} (Sec. C.2), and therefore have zero Fisher norm. Directions that produce a large logit response, and with nonvanishing softmax covariance, give large Fisher eigenvalues, which we bound in the next subsection.

C.5 A lower bound on the largest eigenvalue

Proof of Proposition 2. To reach the top of the spectrum, we do not need to diagonalize SS. It is enough to probe a single, carefully chosen direction. By the Rayleigh quotient, every diagonal element of SS in an orthonormal parameter basis is a lower bound on λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S). It therefore suffices to exhibit one recurrent-bias direction whose diagonal element is large.

Throughout this subsection, SS denotes the population Fisher matrix of Eq. (98), that is, the Ns→∞N_{s}\to\infty limit of Eq. (96). Proposition 2 is therefore a population statement. A finite-sample estimate fluctuates around this population matrix; obtaining a finite-sample analogue of the lower bound would require additional assumptions.

We take the recurrent matrix to be diagonal,

W=diag⁡(r1,…,rdh),W=\operatorname{diag}(r_{1},\dots,r_{d_{h}}), (99)

so that the hidden coordinates no longer mix. Writing the hidden update of Eq. (60) component by component,

(𝐡i)a=ra​(𝐡i−1)a+(V​𝝈i)a+ba,(\mathbf{h}_{i})_{a}=r_{a}\,(\mathbf{h}_{i-1})_{a}+(V\bm{\sigma}_{i})_{a}+b_{a}, (100)

each coordinate evolves on its own. We call the aa-th coordinate hidden mode aa, and rar_{a} its multiplier: a perturbation of that mode is rescaled by rar_{a} at every site, so after kk sites it carries a factor rakr_{a}^{\,k}. This single number controls how fast the response grows. We then perturb only the recurrent bias along one such mode,

d​𝜽=d​𝐛=δ​ba​𝐞a,d\bm{\theta}=d\mathbf{b}=\delta b_{a}\,\mathbf{e}_{a}, (101)

where 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a} is the aa-th standard basis vector of ℝdh\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}. We now linearize the hidden update of Eq. (60). Under a variation of the bias alone, both V​𝝈iV\bm{\sigma}_{i} and WW are held fixed, so the response obeys d​𝐡i=W​d​𝐡i−1+d​𝐛d\mathbf{h}_{i}=W\,d\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+d\mathbf{b}. The initial hidden state is fixed at 𝐡0=𝟎\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}, hence d​𝐡0=𝟎d\mathbf{h}_{0}=\mathbf{0}. Unrolling the recursion from this starting point gives

d​𝐡i−1=∑k=0i−2Wk​d​𝐛,d\mathbf{h}_{i-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}W^{k}\,d\mathbf{b}, (102)

a geometric sum in which the term Wk​d​𝐛W^{k}\,d\mathbf{b} is the bias variation after it has propagated through kk sites.

We now insert this response into the logit map 𝐳i=U​𝐡i−1+𝐜\mathbf{z}_{i}=U\mathbf{h}_{i-1}+\mathbf{c}. Because WW is diagonal, Eq. (99) gives Wk​𝐞a=rak​𝐞aW^{k}\mathbf{e}_{a}=r_{a}^{k}\mathbf{e}_{a}, so every term of the sum stays on mode aa, and the logit response reduces to

d​𝐳i=U​d​𝐡i−1=𝐮a​mi−1​(ra)​δ​ba,𝐮a≡U​𝐞a,\begin{gathered}d\mathbf{z}_{i}=U\,d\mathbf{h}_{i-1}=\mathbf{u}_{a}\,m_{i-1}(r_{a})\,\delta b_{a},\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{u}_{a}\equiv U\mathbf{e}_{a},\end{gathered} (103)

where 𝐮a\mathbf{u}_{a} is the readout of hidden mode aa, that is, the logit direction this mode excites. The geometric factor collects the powers of rar_{a} picked up along the way,

mi−1​(ra)=∑k=0i−2rak.m_{i-1}(r_{a})=\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}r_{a}^{\,k}. (104)

Because the displacement of Eq. (101) has a single nonzero component, the quadratic form reduces to one diagonal element of SS,

d​𝜽𝖳​S​d​𝜽=|δ​ba|2​Sba​ba,d\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,d\bm{\theta}=|\delta b_{a}|^{2}\,S_{b_{a}b_{a}}, (105)

We identify that element by evaluating the right-hand side of Eq. (97) on the logit response of Eq. (103). Both sides then carry the same factor |δ​ba|2|\delta b_{a}|^{2}, which cancels and leaves

Sba​ba=14​∑i=1N|mi−1​(ra)|2​χa,i,χa,i≡⟨𝐮a𝖳​Ci​𝐮a⟩,\begin{gathered}S_{b_{a}b_{a}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|m_{i-1}(r_{a})|^{2}\,\chi_{a,i},\\[2.0pt] \chi_{a,i}\equiv\big\langle\mathbf{u}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}C_{i}\mathbf{u}_{a}\big\rangle,\end{gathered} (106)

Here χa,i\chi_{a,i} is the softmax covariance CiC_{i} of Eq. (90), projected onto the readout direction 𝐮a\mathbf{u}_{a} and averaged over histories. It is nonnegative, χa,i≥0\chi_{a,i}\geq 0, because CiC_{i} is positive semidefinite.

We can now apply the Rayleigh-quotient argument stated at the start of this subsection: for a symmetric SS, the largest eigenvalue is at least as large as any diagonal element in an orthonormal basis. Let 𝐞ba\mathbf{e}_{b_{a}} denote the unit parameter-basis vector along the coordinate bab_{a}; testing SS along this direction gives

λmax​(S)\displaystyle\lambda_{\max}(S) ≥𝐞ba𝖳​S​𝐞ba=Sba​ba\displaystyle\geq\mathbf{e}_{b_{a}}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,\mathbf{e}_{b_{a}}=S_{b_{a}b_{a}}
=14​∑i=1N|mi−1​(ra)|2​χa,i.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|m_{i-1}(r_{a})|^{2}\,\chi_{a,i}. (107)

C.6 Asymptotic scaling of the bound

We now determine how the bound of Eq. (107) grows with the system size NN. The growth is controlled entirely by the geometric factor mi−1​(ra)m_{i-1}(r_{a}), and we treat two regimes. A marginally stable recurrent mode already makes λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S) diverge polynomially in NN, and an expanding mode makes it diverge exponentially.

Marginal mode, ra=1r_{a}=1. Every term of the geometric factor of Eq. (104) equals 1k=11^{k}=1, so the sum counts its i−1i-1 terms,

mi−1​(1)=∑k=0i−21=i−1,m_{i-1}(1)=\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}1=i-1, (108)

and Eq. (106) becomes

Sba​ba=14​∑i=1N(i−1)2​χa,i.S_{b_{a}b_{a}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(i-1)^{2}\,\chi_{a,i}. (109)

The N3N^{3} growth derived below rests on one assumption. The quantity χa,i\chi_{a,i} must be bounded below uniformly, i.e. it must not become arbitrarily small: there must be a constant χ0>0\chi_{0}>0 such that χa,i≥χ0\chi_{a,i}\geq\chi_{0} at every site ii and for every sequence length NN. Since χa,i\chi_{a,i} measures the softmax covariance along the readout direction 𝐮a\mathbf{u}_{a}, this says that the softmax of the unperturbed model must not saturate in that direction.

This assumption is imposed on the unperturbed model; it does not follow from the recurrence multiplier alone. When ra=1r_{a}=1, the derivative of the logits with respect to the recurrent bias accumulates linearly along the chain, as Eq. (108) shows. This derivative growth does not by itself imply that the unperturbed logits grow with ii. Uniform non-saturation is therefore an independent hypothesis. If the unperturbed softmax does saturate, then Ci=diag⁡(𝐩i)−𝐩i​𝐩i𝖳→0C_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{p}_{i})-\mathbf{p}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\to 0 and the lower bound can weaken because χa,i→0\chi_{a,i}\to 0.

Under this assumption we may replace χa,i\chi_{a,i} in Eq. (109) by its lower bound χ0\chi_{0}, which gives Sba​ba≥χ04​∑i=1N(i−1)2S_{b_{a}b_{a}}\geq\tfrac{\chi_{0}}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(i-1)^{2}. The remaining sum has a closed form,

∑i=1N(i−1)2=(N−1)​N​(2​N−1)6∼N33,\sum_{i=1}^{N}(i-1)^{2}=\frac{(N-1)N(2N-1)}{6}\sim\frac{N^{3}}{3}, (110)

and the two prefactors 14\tfrac{1}{4} and 13\tfrac{1}{3} combine to give

λmax​(S)≥Sba​ba≳χ012​N3∼N3,\lambda_{\max}(S)\geq S_{b_{a}b_{a}}\gtrsim\frac{\chi_{0}}{12}\,N^{3}\sim N^{3}, (111)

so the largest eigenvalue grows polynomially with the sequence length.

Expanding mode, |ra|>1|r_{a}|>1. Here ra≠1r_{a}\neq 1, so the finite geometric series of Eq. (104) can be summed in closed form. Its i−1i-1 terms give

mi−1​(ra)=∑k=0i−2rak=1−rai−11−ra.m_{i-1}(r_{a})=\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}r_{a}^{\,k}=\frac{1-r_{a}^{\,i-1}}{1-r_{a}}. (112)

We substitute this into Eq. (106) and again assume that the softmax covariance does not saturate along 𝐮a\mathbf{u}_{a}, so that χa,i≥χ0>0\chi_{a,i}\geq\chi_{0}>0 uniformly. Since every term in Eq. (106) is nonnegative, retaining only the i=Ni=N term gives the rigorous lower bound

Sba​ba\displaystyle S_{b_{a}b_{a}} ≥14​|mN−1​(ra)|2​χa,N\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\,|m_{N-1}(r_{a})|^{2}\,\chi_{a,N}
=14​|1−raN−1|2|1−ra|2​χa,N=Ω⁡(|ra|2​(N−1)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{|1-r_{a}^{\,N-1}|^{2}}{|1-r_{a}|^{2}}\,\chi_{a,N}=\Omega\!\left(|r_{a}|^{2(N-1)}\right), (113)

where the last statement uses χa,N≥χ0\chi_{a,N}\geq\chi_{0} and fixed |ra|>1|r_{a}|>1. Thus Sba​baS_{b_{a}b_{a}} , and therefore λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S), grows at least exponentially in NN.

The asymptotic form mi−1∼rai−1/(ra−1)m_{i-1}\sim r_{a}^{\,i-1}/(r_{a}-1) is needed only to read off the growth of this final retained term. It need not be substituted term by term inside the full sum; at i=1i=1, for instance, the exact value is m0=0m_{0}=0. Two regimes remain, one for each part of the proposition. The first is the marginal case ra=1r_{a}=1: replacing every weight χa,i\chi_{a,i} in Eq. (109) by its uniform lower bound χ0\chi_{0} and evaluating the sum of squares with Eq. (110) gives the bound of Eq. (35), which grows as N3N^{3} (Eq. (111)). The second is the expanding case |ra|>1|r_{a}|>1: the sum in Eq. (107) has only nonnegative terms, so keeping only the i=Ni=N term already gives a valid lower bound at every NN, Eq. (36), and it grows exponentially in NN (Eq. (113)). □\square

C.7 Summary

We now collect the two ends of the spectrum. Together they are what makes SS ill-conditioned. The bottom of the spectrum comes from Sec. C.2. A change of hidden-coordinate basis A∈G​L​(dh)A\in GL(d_{h}) moves the parameters but leaves the wave function unchanged. Along the directions generated by such a change, d​log⁡Ψ=0d\log\Psi=0, and this holds configuration by configuration, not only on average. Since S=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger} is built from the sample-centered log-derivative matrix 𝒪¯\bar{\mathcal{O}}, its quadratic form vanishes along those directions. They are therefore exact zero eigenvalues of SS, at any sample size. These are the Fisher-information singularities.

The top of the spectrum comes from Secs. C.5–C.6. There we probed a single recurrent-bias direction and applied the Rayleigh bound of Eq. (107), which bounds λmax​(S)\lambda_{\max}(S) below by a single diagonal element of SS. How fast that element grows is set by the multiplier rar_{a} of the hidden mode being probed. A marginal mode (ra=1r_{a}=1) gives λmax​(S)≳N3\lambda_{\max}(S)\gtrsim N^{3}, polynomial growth in the sequence length NN; an expanding mode (|ra|>1|r_{a}|>1) gives growth that is exponential in NN. Both statements assume that χa,i\chi_{a,i} stays bounded below by a positive constant, uniformly in the site index ii and in NN.

For the population matrix of the simplified model, an exact gauge zero mode together with a diverging top makes the condition number unbounded. Further small eigenvalues can arise from softmax saturation (Ci→0C_{i}\to 0) and sampling fluctuations. In information-geometry language, the Fisher spectrum encodes the local curvature of the variational manifold. The gauge zero modes are flat, redundant directions; the recurrently amplified modes are strongly curved ones. A broad spectrum therefore reflects a highly anisotropic geometry, precisely the regime that motivates the minSR conditioning strategy used in this work.

Appendix E Training Instabilities

SR and minSR can suffer from instability during training, which manifests as transient spikes in the average local energy [82] or as failures due to NaNs. We find this instability is particularly pronounced at low floating-point precision and when λ\lambda is too small. To understand this, we must look at the condition number κ\kappa of our minSR step, which describes the sensitivity of our solution to noise. For the parameter-space system, define

Sλ≡S+λ​𝕀.S_{\lambda}\equiv S+\lambda\mathbb{I}. (114)

Because SS is positive semidefinite,

κ2​(Sλ)=λmax​(S)+λλmin​(S)+λ.\kappa_{2}(S_{\lambda})=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(S)+\lambda}{\lambda_{\min}(S)+\lambda}. (115)

SS is ill-conditioned, with λmin​(S)=0\lambda_{\min}(S)=0 ( see App. C) so we have

κ2​(Sλ)=1+λmax​(S)λ≈λmax​(S)λ\kappa_{2}(S_{\lambda})=1+\frac{\lambda_{\max}(S)}{\lambda}\approx\frac{\lambda_{\max}(S)}{\lambda} (116)

when λ≪λmax​(S)\lambda\ll\lambda_{\max}(S). The sample-space matrix 𝒯=𝒪¯𝖳′​𝒪¯′\mathcal{T}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime} has the same nonzero eigenvalues as S=𝒪¯′​𝒪¯𝖳′S=\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\prime}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}; hence the same large-eigenvalue scale controls the conditioning of the damped minSR solve.

For a fixed coefficient matrix, perturbation theory for a linear solve gives, to first order in a perturbation of the right-hand side [83, 84]

‖Δ⁡(δ​𝜽)‖2‖δ​𝜽‖2≲κ2​(Sλ)​‖Δ​g‖2‖g‖2.\displaystyle\frac{\|\Delta(\delta\bm{\theta})\|_{2}}{\|\delta\bm{\theta}\|_{2}}\lesssim\kappa_{2}(S_{\lambda})\frac{\|\Delta g\|_{2}}{\|g\|_{2}}. (117)

Thus a standard floating-point estimate for the attainable relative forward accuracy is of order κ2​(Sλ)​εmachine\kappa_{2}(S_{\lambda})\varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}, up to algorithm-dependent constants and additional sampling/model error. When this product is much smaller than one, the corresponding rule-of-thumb number of reliable decimal digits is

d≈−log10⁡(κ2​(Sλ)​εmachine).\displaystyle d\approx-\log_{10}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\!}\big(\kappa_{2}(S_{\lambda})\varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}\big). (118)

Consequently, in the regime λmin​(S)=0\lambda_{\min}(S)=0 and λ≪λmax​(S)\lambda\ll\lambda_{\max}(S), decreasing λ\lambda by one decade costs roughly one decimal digit of numerical accuracy. Additionally, in single floating-point precision, εmachine≈10−7\varepsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}\approx 10^{-7}, which may result in a very small value of dd, leading to instability. This conditioning estimate is consistent with the instability observed in Fig. 6; it should be interpreted as an order-of-magnitude numerical diagnostic rather than as a strict universal error bound.

Appendix F Variance-controlled learning rate for SR

Within the SR setup, a natural (infinitesimal) distance between quantum states is the Fubini–Study distance:

dFS2​(θ,θ+δ​θ)≡1−|⟨Ψθ|Ψθ+δ​θ⟩|2.d_{\mathrm{FS}}^{2}(\theta,\theta+\delta\theta)\equiv 1-\big|\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta+\delta\theta}\rangle\big|^{2}.

For small δ​θ\delta\theta, its second-order expansion is

dFS2​(θ,θ+δ​θ)≈δ​θ𝖳​S​δ​θ,d_{\mathrm{FS}}^{2}(\theta,\theta+\delta\theta)\approx\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}S\,\delta\theta,

where S=Re⁡QS=\operatorname{Re}Q is the SR metric defined in Eq. (31). This yields the trust region constraint

δ​θ𝖳​S​δ​θ≤ε,\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}S\,\delta\theta\leq\varepsilon,

given a small trust-region radius ε\varepsilon. Taylor expanding the energy to first-order,

E⁡(θ+δ​θ)≈E⁡(θ)+g𝖳​δ​θ,gk≡∂E∂θk,E(\theta+\delta\theta)\approx E(\theta)+g^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\theta,\qquad g_{k}\equiv\frac{\partial E}{\partial\theta_{k}},

SR corresponds to the trust-region problem:

minδ​θ⁡g𝖳​δ​θs.t.δ​θ𝖳​S​δ​θ≤ε.\min_{\delta\theta}\;g^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\theta\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}S\,\delta\theta\leq\varepsilon.

The latter, augmented with a Euclidean trust region δ​θ𝖳​δ​θ≤ε′\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\theta\leq\varepsilon^{\prime} that controls the step along the flat directions of SS, can be formulated using the Lagrangian

ℒ⁡(δ​θ,μ,ν)=g𝖳​δ​θ+μ⁡(δ​θ𝖳​S​δ​θ−ε)+ν⁡(δ​θ𝖳​δ​θ−ε′),ν,μ≥0.\mathcal{L}(\delta\theta,\mu,\nu)=g^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\theta+\mu\big(\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}S\delta\theta-\varepsilon\big)+\nu\big(\delta\theta^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\theta-\varepsilon^{\prime}\big),\quad\nu,\mu\geq 0.

Here the first-order condition of optimality (stationarity) in δ​θ\delta\theta gives

∇δ​θℒ=g+2​μ​(S+νμ​𝕀)​δ​θ=0.\nabla_{\delta\theta}\mathcal{L}=g+2\mu\left(S+\frac{\nu}{\mu}\mathbb{I}\right)\delta\theta=0.

Writing η≡12​μ\eta\equiv\frac{1}{2\mu} for the learning rate and λ≡νμ\lambda\equiv\frac{\nu}{\mu}, yields the SR step

δ​θ=−η​(S+λ​𝕀)−1​g.\delta\theta=-\eta\,(S+\lambda\mathbb{I})^{-1}g.

To get the largest step that remains inside the trust region, we impose the constraint:

Appendix G Damping Scheme

The appropriate choice of the damping parameter λ\lambda is essential for stable training. In the derivation of App. F, λ=ν/μ\lambda=\nu/\mu is the ratio of the Lagrange multipliers associated with the Euclidean and Fubini–Study trust-region constraints. Larger λ\lambda therefore suppresses motion in poorly constrained parameter directions more strongly, but λ−1\lambda^{-1} should not be identified with an exact universal trust-region radius. Although a fixed λ\lambda is sufficient for our one-dimensional benchmarks, adaptive damping can be useful more generally, especially in the more ill-conditioned two-dimensional problems. Common schedules use larger damping early in training and smaller damping closer to convergence [85, 86].

Previously introduced methods include a decaying schedule for λ\lambda [1], and an adaptive cutoff based on the signal-to-noise ratio [27]. The LM heuristic is commonly used in Natural Gradients and Gauss-Newton optimization [87] to adjust λ\lambda based on the accuracy of our quadratic model [88, 89]. When a step underperforms, λ\lambda is increased by a factor ω\omega, and when it overperforms, λ\lambda is reduced by a factor of ω−1\omega^{-1}, signaling a higher degree of ‘trust’ in the least-squares solution. We present an implementation of the LM heuristic above.

The LM heuristic interpolates between gradient descent and SR by adjusting λ\lambda at every training step. The ratio ρ\rho is given by [90]

ρ=E𝜽−E𝜽+δ​𝜽E𝜽−[E𝜽+∇E𝜽𝖳δ𝜽+12δ𝜽𝖳Sδ𝜽].\displaystyle\rho=\frac{E_{\bm{\theta}}-E_{\bm{\theta}+\delta\bm{\theta}}}{E_{\bm{\theta}}-\Big[E_{\bm{\theta}}+\nabla E_{\bm{\theta}}^{\mathsf{T}}\delta\bm{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\delta\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\delta\bm{\theta}\Big]}.

The numerator involves the differences in expected energy as defined in Eq. (21). The denominator is an approximation of the numerator with E𝜽+δ​𝜽E_{\bm{\theta}+\delta\bm{\theta}} replaced by a quadratic model about 𝜽\bm{\theta}, in which the QGT SS would play the role of the Hessian of the energy. There is an alternative linear model approach to ρ\rho applied in [89, 88]. The denominator can be simplified as

ρ=E𝜽−E𝜽+δ​𝜽−ϵ¯𝖳′​𝒪¯𝖳′​δ​𝜽−12​η2.\displaystyle\rho=\frac{E_{\bm{\theta}}-E_{\bm{\theta}+\delta\bm{\theta}}}{-\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}\delta\bm{\theta}-\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}}.

The quadratic term simplifies due to our trust region: the step saturates the trust-region constraint of App. F, so δ​𝜽𝖳​S​δ​𝜽=ε=η2\delta\bm{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}S\,\delta\bm{\theta}=\varepsilon=\eta^{2}. This further simplifies to

ρ=E𝜽−E𝜽+δ​𝜽η∗​ϵ¯𝖳′​𝝉−12​η2.\displaystyle\rho=\frac{E_{\bm{\theta}}-E_{\bm{\theta}+\delta\bm{\theta}}}{\eta_{*}\bar{\bm{\epsilon}}^{{}^{\prime}\mathsf{T}}\bm{\tau}-\frac{1}{2}\eta^{2}}.

Then λ\lambda is updated as follows [90]

λ={ω​λ,ρ<14,ω−1​λ,ρ>34,λ,otherwise.\displaystyle\lambda=\begin{cases}\omega\lambda,&\rho<\frac{1}{4},\\ \omega^{-1}\lambda,&\rho>\frac{3}{4},\\ \lambda{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25},}&\textrm{otherwise}.\end{cases} (122)

Here ω>1\omega>1 is a hyperparameter often chosen to be 32\frac{3}{2}.

The LM heuristic requires an additional forward pass to calculate E𝜽+δ​𝜽E_{\bm{\theta}+\delta\bm{\theta}}, though this does not change the runtime significantly since the backward passes dominate the computational cost.

Appendix H Proof of the subsampled-QGT error bound

This appendix proves Proposition 3. The configurations 𝝈(1),…,𝝈(Ns)\bm{\sigma}^{(1)},\dots,\bm{\sigma}^{(N_{s})} are drawn i.i.d. from the Born distribution |Ψ𝜽|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}; exact autoregressive sampling guarantees this independence. For each parameter i=1,…,Npi=1,\dots,N_{p} we write Oi​(𝝈)=∂θilog⁡Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)O_{i}(\bm{\sigma})=\partial_{\theta_{i}}\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) for the log-derivative, which is complex when the ansatz is complex. In the notation of the main text, 𝒪i​s=Oi​(𝝈(s))/Ns\mathcal{O}_{is}=O_{i}(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)})/\sqrt{N_{s}}. We define

μi=𝔼⁡[Oi],Xi=Oi−μi.\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[O_{i}],\qquad X_{i}=O_{i}-\mu_{i}. (123)

Throughout, 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] denotes the expectation and Pr⁡[⋅]\Pr[\cdot] the probability of an event, both taken over the sample draw at fixed 𝜽\bm{\theta}. The two matrices we compare are the population QGT

Qi​j=𝔼⁡[Xi​Xj∗]Q_{ij}=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}X_{j}^{*}] (124)

and its population-centered estimator Q~\widetilde{Q} of Eq. (43); both are Np×NpN_{p}\times N_{p} and Hermitian.

For a complex random variable ZZ we use Var⁡(Z)≡𝔼⁡[|Z−𝔼⁡[Z]|2]\operatorname{Var}(Z)\equiv\mathbb{E}[|Z-\mathbb{E}[Z]|^{2}]. This variance is additive over independent summands, because it equals Var⁡(Re⁡Z)+Var⁡(Im⁡Z)\operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{Re}Z)+\operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{Im}Z) and each real part is additive.

The proof uses exactly two hypotheses: (i) i.i.d. sampling from |Ψ𝜽|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}, and (ii) finiteness of Vavg(c)V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)} in Eq. (44). Hypothesis (ii) is not restrictive. Since Var⁡(Xi​Xj∗)≤𝔼⁡[|Xi|2​|Xj|2]\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}X_{j}^{*})\leq\mathbb{E}[|X_{i}|^{2}|X_{j}|^{2}] and, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, 𝔼⁡[|Xi|2​|Xj|2]≤𝔼⁡[|Xi|4]​𝔼​[|Xj|4]\mathbb{E}[|X_{i}|^{2}|X_{j}|^{2}]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[|X_{i}|^{4}]\,\mathbb{E}[|X_{j}|^{4}]}, it holds whenever the centered log-derivatives have finite fourth moments under |Ψ𝜽|2|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}|^{2}.

Proof of Proposition 3. The estimator is an average of one term per sample, so its error is pure sampling noise. We follow that noise from a single entry, to the whole matrix, and finally into a probability.

We start by establishing unbiasedness. Define the per-sample product

Yi​j(s)=Xi​(𝝈(s))​Xj​(𝝈(s))∗,Y_{ij}^{(s)}=X_{i}\big(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}\big)\,X_{j}\big(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}\big)^{*}, (125)

so that Q~i​j=1Ns​∑sYi​j(s)\widetilde{Q}_{ij}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s}Y_{ij}^{(s)} by Eq. (43). The samples are identically distributed, so 𝔼⁡[Yi​j(s)]=Qi​j\mathbb{E}[Y_{ij}^{(s)}]=Q_{ij} for every ss. Linearity of expectation then gives 𝔼⁡[Q~i​j]=Qi​j\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Q}_{ij}]=Q_{ij}: the estimator is unbiased, and its error is exactly the fluctuation of the average about its mean.

Because the estimator is unbiased, that fluctuation is measured by the variance of each entry. Fix (i,j)(i,j). The terms Yi​j(1),…,Yi​j(Ns)Y_{ij}^{(1)},\dots,Y_{ij}^{(N_{s})} are functions of independent samples, hence independent, and each has the single-sample variance Var⁡(Xi​Xj∗)\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}X_{j}^{*}), finite by hypothesis (ii). Additivity of the variance together with the scaling Var⁡(c​Z)=|c|2​Var⁡(Z)\operatorname{Var}(cZ)=|c|^{2}\operatorname{Var}(Z) gives

Var⁡(Q~i​j)\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\big(\widetilde{Q}_{ij}\big) =1Ns2​∑s=1NsVar⁡(Yi​j(s))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{s}^{2}}\sum_{s=1}^{N_{s}}\operatorname{Var}\big(Y_{ij}^{(s)}\big)
=1Ns​Var⁡(Xi​Xj∗).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\,\operatorname{Var}\big(X_{i}X_{j}^{*}\big). (126)

Averaging NsN_{s} independent copies divides the variance by NsN_{s}; this single factor 1/Ns1/N_{s} is the only source of NsN_{s}-dependence in the bound.

Summing these entrywise variances produces the expected squared error of the whole matrix. By definition ‖A‖F2=∑i,j|Ai​j|2\|A\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^{2}, and unbiasedness turns each summand into a variance, 𝔼⁡[|Q~i​j−Qi​j|2]=Var⁡(Q~i​j)\mathbb{E}[|\widetilde{Q}_{ij}-Q_{ij}|^{2}]=\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde{Q}_{ij}). Summing Eq. (126) over all Np2N_{p}^{2} pairs and inserting Eq. (44) yields

𝔼⁡[‖Q~−Q‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}^{2}] =1Ns​∑i,j=1NpVar⁡(Xi​Xj∗)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N_{p}}\operatorname{Var}\big(X_{i}X_{j}^{*}\big)
=Np2Ns​Vavg(c).\displaystyle=\frac{N_{p}^{2}}{N_{s}}\,V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}. (127)

The factor Np2N_{p}^{2} counts the entries, and the 1/Ns1/N_{s} carries over unchanged from each of them.

A high-probability bound now follows from Markov’s inequality. Since ‖Q~−Q‖F2\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}^{2} is nonnegative, for any t>0t>0

Pr[∥Q~−Q∥F≥t]\displaystyle\Pr\big[\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}\geq t\big] =Pr[∥Q~−Q∥F2≥t2]\displaystyle=\Pr\big[\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}^{2}\geq t^{2}\big]
≤𝔼⁡[‖Q~−Q‖F2]t2=Np2​Vavg(c)Ns​t2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}^{2}]}{t^{2}}=\frac{N_{p}^{2}\,V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}}{N_{s}\,t^{2}}, (128)

where the first equality holds because squaring is monotone on nonnegative reals. Choosing

t=NpNs​Vavg(c)ϵt=\frac{N_{p}}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\sqrt{\frac{V_{\mathrm{avg}}^{(c)}}{\epsilon}} (129)

makes the right-hand side of Eq. (128) equal to ϵ\epsilon. The reverse inequality ‖Q~−Q‖F<t\|\widetilde{Q}-Q\|_{F}<t is exactly Eq. (46), so it holds with probability at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. The square root taken here is what turns the entrywise factor 1/Ns1/N_{s} into the Ns−1/2N_{s}^{-1/2} rate carried by the norm.

The spectral norm inherits the same bound. For any matrix AA, ‖A‖22\|A\|_{2}^{2} is the largest squared singular value, while ‖A‖F2\|A\|_{F}^{2} is the sum of all of them; hence ‖A‖2≤‖A‖F\|A\|_{2}\leq\|A\|_{F}, and Eq. (46) also bounds ‖Q−Q~‖2\|Q-\widetilde{Q}\|_{2}.

For real variational parameters, the population SR metric is S=Re⁡QS=\operatorname{Re}Q. Defining S~=Re⁡Q~\widetilde{S}=\operatorname{Re}\widetilde{Q}, we have

‖S−S~‖F=‖Re⁡(Q−Q~)‖F≤‖Q−Q~‖F,\|S-\widetilde{S}\|_{F}=\|\operatorname{Re}(Q-\widetilde{Q})\|_{F}\leq\|Q-\widetilde{Q}\|_{F}, (130)

so the same bound applies to the SR metric.

The proof never assumed that Ψ𝜽\Psi_{\bm{\theta}} is real or positive. Every step relied only on linearity of 𝔼\mathbb{E}, on the additivity of Var⁡(Z)=𝔼⁡[|Z−𝔼⁡[Z]|2]\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\mathbb{E}[|Z-\mathbb{E}[Z]|^{2}] over independent terms, and on hypothesis (ii). The same QGT bound therefore applies to complex RNN wave functions (cRNN) just as it does to positive ones (pRNN). □\square

Sample-mean centering. Proposition 3 uses the population-centered estimator Q~\widetilde{Q}, in which the exact population mean μi=𝔼⁡[Oi]\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[O_{i}] is subtracted. In practice, we use the sample-centered matrix Q^=𝒪¯​𝒪¯†\widehat{Q}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}\bar{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}, in which each log-derivative has its sample mean

μ^i=1Ns​∑sOi​(𝝈(s))\hat{\mu}_{i}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s}O_{i}(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}) (131)

subtracted. We now check that this sample centering does not change the Ns−1/2N_{s}^{-1/2} rate. Since

𝝁^−𝝁=1Ns​∑s𝑿⁡(𝝈(s)),\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{s}\bm{X}\big(\bm{\sigma}^{(s)}\big), (132)

multiplying out the sample-centered products gives

Q^=Q~−(𝝁^−𝝁)​(𝝁^−𝝁)†.\widehat{Q}=\widetilde{Q}-(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})^{\dagger}. (133)

Subtracting QQ gives

Q^−Q=(Q~−Q)−(𝝁^−𝝁)​(𝝁^−𝝁)†.\widehat{Q}-Q=\big(\widetilde{Q}-Q\big)-(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})^{\dagger}. (134)

The first difference is controlled by Proposition 3. For the second, the rank-one identity ‖𝒙​𝒚†‖F=‖𝒙‖2​‖𝒚‖2\|\bm{x}\bm{y}^{\dagger}\|_{F}=\|\bm{x}\|_{2}\|\bm{y}\|_{2} gives

‖(𝝁^−𝝁)​(𝝁^−𝝁)†‖F=‖𝝁^−𝝁‖22.\big\|(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})^{\dagger}\big\|_{F}=\|\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}. (135)

The mean correction is therefore governed by ‖𝝁^−𝝁‖22\|\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}, and 𝝁^\hat{\bm{\mu}} is itself an i.i.d. average:

𝔼⁡[‖𝝁^−𝝁‖22]=1Ns​∑i=1NpVar⁡(Oi),\mathbb{E}\left[\|\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu}\|_{2}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{p}}\operatorname{Var}(O_{i}), (136)

where the last sum runs over all parameter indices. Thus, if the average variance per parameter remains O⁡(1)O(1) as NpN_{p} varies, this term scales linearly with NpN_{p}. The correction due to sample-mean centering is therefore of order Ns−1N_{s}^{-1} in expectation and is subleading to the Ns−1/2N_{s}^{-1/2} fluctuation bounded in Proposition 3. Thus sample centering does not change the leading rate.

A few further remarks complete the picture. First, at finite NsN_{s} the sample-centered estimator has a small, non-random bias. Using

𝔼⁡[(𝝁^−𝝁)​(𝝁^−𝝁)†]=QNs\mathbb{E}\left[(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})(\hat{\bm{\mu}}-\bm{\mu})^{\dagger}\right]=\frac{Q}{N_{s}} (137)

gives

𝔼⁡[Q^]=Ns−1Ns​Q,\mathbb{E}[\widehat{Q}]=\frac{N_{s}-1}{N_{s}}Q, (138)

a bias of −Q/Ns-Q/N_{s}; because it scales as 1/Ns1/N_{s}, it is smaller than the Ns−1/2N_{s}^{-1/2} random fluctuation.

Second, for a normalized ansatz, ∑𝝈|Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)|2=1\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}|\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2}=1, the mean log-derivative has zero real part, Re⁡𝔼⁡[∂θilog⁡Ψ𝜽]=0\operatorname{Re}\mathbb{E}[\partial_{\theta_{i}}\log\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}]=0; for a positive ansatz (pRNN) the mean vanishes entirely, 𝝁=𝟎\bm{\mu}=\bm{0}.

Finally, in Fig. 5(b) the reference matrix is itself an estimate from a finite sample with Ns≳NpN_{s}\gtrsim N_{p}. By the triangle inequality, the measured error contains contributions from both sample sizes; when the reference sample size is sufficiently large, its contribution is smaller, and the leading Ns−1/2N_{s}^{-1/2} rate is unchanged.
